question: 1. After Quit India Movement, C. Rajagopalachari issued a pamphlet entitled ‘The Way Out’. Which one of the following was a proposal in this pamphlet?
options: The establishment of a “War Advisory Council” composed of representatives of British India and the Indian States.
Reconstitution of the Central Executive Council in such a way that all its members, except the Governor General and the Commander-in-Chief, should be Indian leaders.
Fresh elections to the Central and Provincial Legislatures to be held at the end of 1945 and the Constitution-making body be convened as soon as possible.
explanation:
Exp) Option d is the correct answer.
C. Rajagopalachari, also known as Rajaji, was a prominent leader of the Indian National Congress and a close associate of Mahatma Gandhi. He issued a pamphlet entitled ‘The Way Out’ in 1944, in which he proposed a solution to the Constitutional deadlock that had arisen due to the British government's refusal to grant independence to India and the Muslim League’s demand for a separate state of Pakistan for the Muslims of India.

Important Tips

Rajaji’s proposal, which came to be known as the CR Formula or the Rajaji Formula, was as follows:
The Muslim League should endorse the Indian demand for independence and cooperate with the Congress in forming a provisional interim government for a transitional period.
After the end of the Second World War, a commission should be appointed to demarcate the districts having a Muslim majority population in the north-west and eastern zones of India.
The people of these districts should then decide by a plebiscite whether they wanted to forma separate sovereign state or remain with the Indian Union.
The terms of the treaty between the two states should include clauses for safeguarding the rights and interests of the minorities, ensuring free movement and trade, and maintaining common defense and foreign affairs.

subject: Modern History
question: 1. Who among the following drafted the fundamental rights resolution for the Karachi Session of Congress in 1931?
explanation:
Exp) Option b is the correct answer.
Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru drafted the fundamental rights resolution and economic program for the Karachi Session of the Indian National Congress in 1931. The resolution was adopted by the Congress and became an important milestone in the struggle for India’s independence. The resolution outlined a number of fundamental rights that the Congress believed should be guaranteed to all Indians.

Important Tips

The Karachi Session 1931, declared that any Constitution which may be agreed to on its behalf should provide, or enable the Swaraj Government to provide, for the following:
Fundamental Rights and Duties:

  1. Every citizen of India has the right of free expression of opinion, the rights of free association and combination, and the right to assemble peacefully and without arms, for purposes not opposed to law or morality.
    2 Every citizen shall enjoy freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess and practise his religion, subject to public order and morality.
    3 The culture, language and script of the minorities and of the different linguistic areas shall be protected.
    4 All citizens are equal before the law, irrespective of caste, creed or sex.
    5 No disability attaches to any citizen, by reason of his or her religion, caste, creed or sex, in regard to public employment, office of power or honour, and in the exercise of any trade or calling.
    6 All citizens have equal rights and duties in regard to wells, tanks, roads, schools and places of public resort, maintained out of State or local funds, or dedicated by private persons for the use of the general public.
    7 . Every citizen has the right to keep and bear arms, in accordance with regulations and reservations made in that behalf.
    8 No person shall be deprived of his liberty nor shall his dwelling or property be entered, sequestered or confiscated, save in accordance with law.
    9 The State shall observe neutrality in regard to all religions.
    10 The franchise shall be on the basis of universal adult suffrage.
    11 The State shall provide for free and compulsory primary education.
  2. The State shall confer no titles.
    13 There shall be no capital punishment.
  3. Every citizen is free to move throughout India and to stay and settle in any part thereof, to acquire property and to follow any trade or calling, and to be treated equally with regard to legal prosecution or protection in all parts of India.
    Labour
  4. (a) The organisation of economic life must conform to the principle of justice, to the end that it may secure a decent standard of living.
    (b) The State shall safeguard the interests of industrial workers and shall secure for them, by suitable legislation and in other ways, a living wage, healthy conditions of work, limited hours of labour, suitable machinery for the settlement of disputes between employers and workmen and — protection against the economic consequences of old age, sickness and unemployment.
  5. Labour to be freed from serfdom and conditions bordering on serfdom.
  6. Protection of women workers, and specially, adequate provision for leave during maternity period.
    5, Children of school going age shall not be employed in mines and factories.
  7. Peasants and workers shall have the right to form unions to protect their interests.
    Taxation and Expenditure
  8. The system of land tenure and revenue and rent shall be reformed and an equitable adjustment made of the burden on agricultural land, immediately giving relief to the small peasantry by a substantial reduction of agricultural rent and revenue now paid by them, and in ease of uneconomic holdings, exempting them from rent, so long as necessary, with such relief as may be just and necessary, to holders of small estates affected by such exemption or reduction in rent, and to the same end, imposing a graded tax on net income from land above a reasonable minimum.
  9. Death duties on a graduated scale shall be levied on property above a fixed minimum.
  10. There shall be a drastic reduction of Military expenditure so as to bring it down to at least one-half of the present scale.
  11. Expenditure and salaries in civil departments shall be largely reduced. No servant of the State, other than specially employed experts and the like, shall be paid above a certain fixed figure, which should not ordinarily exceed Rs. 500 per month.
  12. No duty shall be levied on salt manufactured in India.
    Economic and Social Programme
  13. The State shall protect indigenous cloth; and for this purpose pursue the policy of exclusion of foreign cloth and foreign yarn from the country and adopt such other measures as may be found necessary. The State shall also protect other indigenous industries, when necessary, against foreign competition.
  14. Intoxicating drinks, and drags shall be totally prohibited, except for medicinal purposes.
  15. Currency and exchange shall be regulated in the national interest.
  16. The State shall own or control key industries and services, mineral resources, railways, waterways, shipping and other means of transport.
  17. Relief of. agricultural indebtedness, and control of usury — direct and indirect.
  18. The State shall provide for the Military training of citizens so as to organise a means of national defence apart from the regular Military forces.

question: 1. During the Indian Freedom Struggle, who of the following raised an army called ‘Free Indian Legion’?
explanation:
Exp) Option c is the correct answer.
During the Indian Freedom Struggle, Subhas Chandra Bose raised an army called the ‘Free Indian Legion’. The legion was intended to serve as a liberation force for British ruled India and was made up of Indian prisoners of war and expatriates in Europe. Subhas Chandra Bose initiated the formation of this legion as part of his efforts to win India’s independence by seeking support from Axis powers during World War II.

Important Tips

Free India Legion:
The Indian Legion, also known as the Free India Legion or Azad Hind Legion, was a military unit raised during World War II.
Formation and Purpose: The Indian Legion was formed in 1941 by Subhas Chandra Bose, an Indian independence leader, during World War II.
Origins: It originated in Berlin as part of Bose’s efforts to gain support for India’s independence struggle by seeking aid from Axis powers.
Composition: The legion comprised Indian prisoners of war and expatriates in Europe, including volunteers from Indian students in Germany and some prisoners of war from North Africa.
Role: Initially intended as an assault group for a German-Indian joint invasion of British India, its primary purpose shifted over time.
Actions: A portion of the Indian Legion was transferred to the Indian National Army in Southeast Asia, while others served non-combat duties in the Netherlands and France.
Engagements: It saw action during the Allied advance across France, primarily against the French Resistance, and a company was sent to Italy in 1944.

No special provisions were made for the representation of depressed classes in the local bodies or appointment to the public services in the Poona Pact.

  • In 1903, Hasrat Mohani started the magazine ‘Urdu-e-Mualla’ in Aligarh, which published articles against imperialist oppression and policies, promoting awareness about the freedom struggle.
  • Due to his activism, he was imprisoned again in 1907, and his magazine was banned by the British authorities. He was an active member of Congress until 1907, closely associated with Bal Gangadhar Tilak.
  • He is credited by some historians with writing the slogan ‘Inquilab Zindabad’ in 1921, a slogan later immortalized by Bhagat Singh.

question: 1. An important aspect of the Cripps Mission of 1942 was:
options: that all Indian States should join the Indian Union as a condition to consider any degree of autonomy for India.
the creation of an Indian Union with Dominion status after the Second World War.

the active participation and cooperation of the Indian People, communities and political parties in the British war efforts as a condition for granting Independence with full Sovereign status to India after the war.
the framing of a constitution for the entire Indian Union, with no separate constitution for any province, and a Union Constitution to be accepted by all provinces.
explanation:
Exp) Option b is the correct answer
In order to get the support of India in World War II, Cripps Mission was sent to India in 1942. Few proposals of this mission are:

  • Setting up of an Indian dominion. This dominion would have the freedom to remain with the British Commonwealth or to secede from it. It would also be at liberty to take part in international organisations.
  • A Constituent Assembly would be formed to frame a new constitution for the country. This Assembly would have members elected by the provincial assemblies and also nominated by the princes.
  • Any province unwilling to join the Indian dominion could form a separate union and have a separate constitution.
  • The transfer of power and the rights of minorities would be safeguarded by negotiations between the Constituent Assembly and the British government.
  • In the meantime, until this new constitution came into force, India’s defence would be controlled by the British and the powers of the Governor-General would remain unaltered.

The adoption of communist revolutionist ideology for political and social reform.
The Pathan regional nationalist unity and a struggle against colonialism.
explanation:
Exp) Option d is the correct answer.
The Khudai Khidmatgars, also known as Red Shirts, were a nonviolent Pashtun nationalist movement in the North-West Frontier Province (now Khyber Pakhtunkhwa) of British India. They were led by Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, also known as Badshah Khan. The Khudai Khidmatgars called for the Pathan regional nationalist unity and a struggle against colonialism. They opposed the British rule in India and they also opposed the partition of India. They were known for their nonviolent methods of protest, such as boycotts, strikes, and civil disobedience.

V. Alexander (First Lord of the Admiralty). The Cabinet Mission put forward its own proposals in May 1946, which included the idea of a Federal Union composed of British provinces and princely states, with a common center for defense, foreign affairs and communications. The Cabinet Mission hoped that this plan would preserve the unity of India and accommodate the demands of the Muslim League for a separate homeland. However, the plan was rejected by both the Congress and the Muslim League, and eventually led to the partition of India in 1947.

explanation:
Exp) Option c is the correct answer.
The Cabinet Mission Plan did not accept the demand of the Muslim League for a separate homeland for the Muslims in India. Instead, it proposed a federal structure with three groups of provinces, each having a high degree of autonomy. The Muslim-majority provinces would form Group B and Group C, while the Hindu-majority provinces would form Group A.
The groups could decide their own internal affairs, but the center would have control over defense, foreign affairs and communications. The Muslim League initially accepted the plan, hoping that it would pave the way for Pakistan in the future, but later rejected it when it realized that the grouping was not compulsory and that the provinces could opt out of the groups after the first general election. The Congress also rejected the plan, as it wanted a strong central government and opposed the idea of grouping. Therefore, the Cabinet Mission Plan failed to resolve the constitutional deadlock and ultimately led to the partition of India in 1947.

question: 1. The Commander-in-Chief of the Indian Army during Quit India Movement was:
explanation:
Exp) Option a is the correct answer.
Lord Wavell was the commander-in-chief of the Indian Army during the Quit India Movement, which was launched by Mahatma Gandhi on 8 August 1942 in Bombay. The movement demanded an immediate end to British rule in India and sanctioned a civil disobedience movement against British authority. The British responded by arresting tens of thousands of leaders and activists, including Gandhi, and unleashing violence on the masses. The movement ended in 1945 with the release of the jailed freedom fighters and the realization by the British that India was no longer governable by them.

Important Tips

  • Lord Wavell: He was a British field marshal and colonial administrator who served as the Viceroy of India from 1943 to 1947. He was responsible for organizing the Simla Conference in 1945, which aimed to reach a consensus among the Indian political parties on the constitutional reforms. He also proposed the Wavell Plan, which envisaged the formation of an executive council with equal representation of Hindus and Muslims, and a balanced representation of other minorities.
  • Lord Mountbatten: He was a British statesman, naval officer, and cousin of King George VI. He served as the last Viceroy of India and the first Governor-General of independent India from 1947 to 1948. He was tasked with overseeing the British withdrawal from India and ensuring a smooth transition to power. However, he also presided over the partition of India into India and Pakistan, which resulted in widespread violence and displacement of millions of people. He was also involved in the negotiations for the accession of princely states to either India or Pakistan. He resigned as Governor-General in 1948 and returned to Britain, where he continued his naval career and became the Chief of Defence Staff.

Important Tips

Sir T.B. Sapru:

  • Tej Bahadur Sapru (1875 -1949) was an Indian freedom fighter, lawyer, and politician. He was a key figure in India’s struggle for independence, helping draft the Indian Constitution. He was the leader of the Liberal party in British-ruled India.
  • He was knighted in 1922 and after receiving knighthood he was known as sir Tej Bahadur Sapru.

  • He became a member of the Privy Council in 1934 and represented the Liberal Party in the Round Table Conferences in London.
  • Sapru supported India’s participation in the Second World War without prior consultation with Indians, a stance that differed from most Indian political activists at the time.

explanation:
Exp) Option a is the correct answer.
The Non-Cooperation resolution was moved by Chittaranjan Das (C.R. Das) during the Nagpur session of the Indian National Congress in 1920. This session marked a significant shift in the Congress's approach to the freedom struggle, as it decided to pursue Swaraj (self-government) through non-cooperation with the British authorities, boycotting foreign goods, schools, and institutions. This approach was intended to be a peaceful and legitimate means of achieving independence.

Important Tips

1920 INC Annual Session:
The Indian National Congress (INC) held its annual session in December 1920 in Nagpur, Maharashtra, with C. Vijayaraghavachariar presiding. This pivotal session saw the adoption of the main resolution on Non-Cooperation, which advocated for:

  • Boycott of Foreign Goods, Schools, and Courts: The resolution urged Indians to boycott British goods, institutions, and the legal system.
  • Surrender of Titles: Indians were encouraged to give up honorary titles bestowed by the British government as a sign of non-cooperation.
  • Harmony Between Muslims and Hindus: The session emphasized promoting unity and understanding between the two major communities.
  • Congress Working Committee: The formation of a 15-member committee to guide the Congress's activities was a significant outcome.
  • Shift in Approach: The session marked a shift from constitutional means to achieving Swaraj (self-government) to a peaceful, non-cooperative mass struggle.
    This session’s reforms elevated the INC’s political standing, shaping a new era in the freedom struggle’s history. The Congress’s commitment to non-cooperation and its emphasis on unity set the stage for transformative actions in India’s fight for independence.

  2. It was appointed to enquire into the working of the 1919 Act.
  3. It was headed by Sir John Simon.

  5. It was opposed by the Indian leaders
    Select the correct answer using the code given below:
explanation:
Exp) Option d is the correct answer.
Statement 1 is correct: The Simon Commission, formally known as the Indian Statutory Commission, was indeed appointed to review and enquire into the working of the Government of India Act of 1919. The purpose was to assess the reforms that had been implemented and to make recommendations for potential further reforms.
Statement 2 is correct: It was chaired by Sir John Simon. He was a British politician and lawyer who led the commission during its study of the constitutional framework in India.
Statement 3 is correct: Simon Commission advocated for a Federation-style structure at the centre, with a ‘Council of Greater India’ representing the interests of both British India and the princely states.
Statement 4 is correct: Yes, the Simon Commission faced significant opposition from Indian leaders and political parties. The main reasons for opposition included the fact that the commission did not have any Indian members and its recommendations were geen as inadequate in addressing Indian demands for self-governance and representation.

Important Tips

Recommendations of Simon Commission:

  • Abolish Provincial Dyarchy: Expand ministers’ responsibilities to provincial legislatures, eliminating the system of dual control.
  • Governor’s Special Powers: Grant the Governor special powers to protect minorities and safeguard provinces.
  • Representation based on Population: Advocate representation in the Federal Assembly based on population.
  • Burma’s Dominion Status: Grant Burma Dominion Status and its own Constitution.
  • Council of State Representation: Propose indirect election of Council of State members through Provincial Councils, akin to modern Proportional Representation.
  • Federation-style Structure: Suggest 4 ‘Council of Greater India to represent British India and princely states.
  • Reservations for Poorest Classes: Recommend reserved seats for the economically disadvantaged.

Parallel governments were established in Balia and Satara during the Quit India Movement. The Quit India Movement, also known as the August Movement, was a mass civil disobedience campaign launched by Mahatma Gandhi and the Indian National Congress in 1942, demanding an end to British colonial rule in India.

Important Tips

Parrallel Governments in 1942:

  • Four major parallel governments were established in Balliya (Uttar Pradesh), Tamluk (Bengal), Satara (Maharashtra) and Talcher (Orissa).
  • In Balia, a district in Uttar Pradesh, a parallel government was formed on 19 August 1942 by Chitta Pandey, a freedom fighter and a Congress leader. He declared Balia as independent and appointed his own cabinet of ministers. He also issued his own currency and stamps, collected taxes, ran courts, and maintained law and order. He also organized a volunteer army to resist the British forces. The parallel government lasted for about a month, until the British army recaptured Balia on 23 September 1942.
  • In Satara, a district in Maharashtra, a parallel government was formed on 10 September 1942 by Nana Patil, another freedom fighter and a Congress leader. He was inspired by the example of Balia and decided to replicate it in Satara. He declared Satara as independent and appointed his own cabinet of ministers.
  • In Tamluk in Midnapur district, parallel government, known as Jatiya Sarkar, was established on December 17, 1942. It lasted until September 1944.
  • In Talcher in Orissa, parallel government was established in 1943 by some local Congress workers. They took control of the police station and declared independence from British rule.

The Mountbatten Plan was a plan for the transfer of power from British rule to Indian rule in 1947. It was announced by Lord Mountbatten, the last Viceroy of India, on June 3, 1947. The plan called for the partition of British India into two dominions, a Hindu-majority India and a Muslim majority Pakistan. The Mountbatten Plan was accepted by the Indian National Congress and the Muslim League, and it was approved by the British Parliament. The plan came into effect on August 15, 1947, when India and Pakistan became independent dominions.

Important Tips

The Mountbatten Plan’s Provisions were as follows:

  • British India would be divided into two dominions: India and Pakistan.
  • The constitution drafted by the Constituent Assembly would not be applicable to Muslim-majority areas, as they would become part of Pakistan.
  • According to the plan, the legislative assemblies of Bengal and Punjab convened and voted in favor of partition.
  • The legislative assembly of Sind would make the choice of joining the Indian constituent assembly or not. It opted to join Pakistan.
  • A referendum was scheduled for NWFP (North-Western Frontier Province) to determine its dominion affiliation. NWEP chose to join Pakistan, although Khan Abdul Gaffar Khan boycotted and rejected the referendum.
  • The transfer of power was set for August 15, 1947.
  • To delineate the international boundaries between the two nations, the Boundary Commission was established, with Sir Cyril Radcliffe serving as its chairperson. The commission was tasked with demarcating Bengal and Punjab into the two new countries.

Statement 1 is correct: The Third Round Table Conference was held from November 17 to December 24, 1932, in London.

    Statement 2 is correct: After the Round Table Conferences ended without reaching consensus with Indian leaders, the British Government unilaterally moved ahead.
  • The White Paper on Constitutional Reform (1933) was prepared based on discussions held in all three Round Table Conferences.
  • A Joint Select Committee of the British Parliament examined the White Paper proposals between 1933-1934.
  • Based on its recommendations, the Government of India Act, 1935 was drafted and passed by the British Parliament.
  • Itbecame the longest act ever passed by British Parliament and the basis of Indian administration until 1947 (and even later for Pakistan until 1956).
    Statement 3 is incorrect: In reality, Provincial Autonomy was a major feature of the Act.
  • The Act abolished diarchy in provinces (which was introduced by the Government of India Act, 1919) and instead established responsible government at the provincial level.
  • Provincial Legislatures were to be elected, and Indian ministers were made responsible to them.
  • Provinces were granted autonomous powers, except in areas such as defense, external affairs, and communications, which remained with the Centre.
  • 11 provinces were set up with their own Legislative Assemblies and Councils of Ministers.
    Statement 4 is incorrect: Though provincial autonomy was introduced, British control was maintained through discretionary powers vested in the Governor. The Governor retained “special responsibilities” and was empowered to:
  • Override the advice of ministers.
  • Reserve bills for consideration by the Governor-General or British authorities.
  • Take over the administration in case of breakdown of constitutional machinery.

She was born on 22 December 1924 in Barangabari village of Gohpur subdivision in Assam. She was inspired by the freedom struggle and joined the Mrityu Bahini (Death Squad), a group of young volunteers who were ready to sacrifice their lives for the cause of independence.
On 20 September 1942, she led a group of about 500 people, mostly women and children, who marched towards the Gohpur police station with the intention of hoisting the Indian National flag there. When they reached near the police station, they were stopped by a British officer named R.S. Linton, who ordered them to disperse. He also threatened to shoot them if they did not obey. Kanaklata refused to turn back and continued to move forward with the flag in her hand. She said, “We are not afraid of death. We are ready to die for our country.” Linton then opened fire at the unarmed crowd, killing Kanaklata and another volunteer named Mukunda Kakoti on the spot.

Important Tips

Naujawan Bharat Sabha (NBS):

  • Naujawan Bharat Sabha (NBS) was founded in March 1926 by Bhagat Singh as a left-wing Indian association.
  • It aimed to foment revolution against British colonial rule by mobilizing worker and peasant youths and promoting Marxist ideas.
  • NBS was closely associated with the Hindustan Republican Association and merged with the All India Youth Federation (AIYF) of the Communist Party of India later.
  • The organization had members from Hindu, Muslim, and Sikh communities and conducted lectures, public meetings, and protests.

Exp) Option c is the correct answer.
In February 1947, Prime Minister Clement Atlee announced in the House of Commons that the British Government intended to transfer power to India by June 1948. To facilitate this transition, Lord Mountbatten was appointed as India’s Viceroy on March 24, 1947, with extensive powers. Recognizing the likelihood of India’s partition and the creation of Pakistan, Lord Mountbatten proposed the partition plan on June 3, 1947, known as the Mountbatten Plan. According to this plan, Punjab and Bengal Legislative Assemblies would vote on partition in separate groups, allowing Hindus and Muslims to make their choices. Sindh would make its own decision, while a referendum in the North-West Frontier Province (now known as Khyber Pakhtunwa) and Sylhet district of Assam was scheduled to resolve their status. question: 1. During the Quit India Movement parallel ‘National Government was established at many places. Which of the following is not correctly matched?
explanation:
Exp) Option a is the correct answer.
Option a is incorrect. During the Quit India Movement of 1942, several regions in India witnessed the formation of parallel or alternative governments, as a form of defiance against British rule. There is no evidence of a “Raiyati Sarkar” being established in Kheda, Gujarat during the Quit India Movement.
Option b is correct. The Prati Sarkar (“Parallel Government”) in Satara, Maharashtra was one of the most organized and well-known parallel governments during the Quit India Movement. It was led by leaders like Krantisinh Nana Patil and involved establishing people’s courts, police, and administrative services.
Option c is correct. In Talcher, a princely state in Orissa (now Odisha), the Praja Mandal, a parallel government was established during the Quit India period. The Praja Mandal was a type of people’s organization that challenged the autocratic rule of local princes and demanded integration with democratic India.
Option d is correct. The Jatiy Sarkar (National Government) was established in Tamluk, Bengal, in 1942 during the Quit India Movement. It functioned as a parallel government for nearly two years, managing law and order, judicial work, relief efforts, and education.

Important tips

Quit India Movement (1942):

  • Launched on 8 August 1942 by the Indian National Congress at the Bombay session, following the failure of the Cripps Mission.
  • Mahatma Gandhi gave the clarion call of “Do or Die”, urging Indians to force the British to “Quit India”.
  • The movement aimed at the immediate end of British rule in India.
  • Within hours of the launch, top Congress leaders (including Gandhi, Nehru, Patel) were arrested, leaving the movement to be led by local leaders and the masses.
  • It became a massive, decentralized movement, involving strikes, protests, sabotage, and civil disobedience across the country.
  • British repression was brutal, with mass arrests, lathi charges, shootings, and censorship of the press.
  • Though unsuccessful in achieving immediate freedom, the movement clearly showed that the British could no longer govern without Indian support.

subject: Modern History
question: 1. In which Session Indian National Congress passed Complete Independence Resolution?
explanation:
Exp) Option c is the correct answer.
The Indian National Congress passed the Complete Independence Resolution at its Lahore session in 1929. This historic resolution, also known as the ‘Purna Swaraj’ resolution, declared the goal of achieving total independence for India. It was a response to the breakdown of negotiations with the British over dominion status. The Lahore session led by Jawaharlal Nehru marked a turning point in the freedom movement, advocating civil disobedience and celebrating January 26, 1930, as the first Independence Day.

Important Tips

Nagpur Congess Session-1920: The Indian National Congress held its annual session in December 1920 in Nagpur, presided over by C. Vijayaraghavachariar. It marked a turning point as the INC adopted the Non-Cooperation Resolution, advocating boycott of foreign goods, schools, and courts, and promoting Hindu-Muslim harmony. The session established a 15-member Congress Working Committee, shifting focus from constitutional means to extraconstitutional peaceful struggle for Swaraj.
Belgaum Congess Session-1924: The 39th session of the Indian National Congress held at Belgaum in 1924 was the only Congress session presided over by Mahatma Gandhi. Theater performances like “Pavitra Khadi,” promoting Gandhian ideals, were staged, fostering nationalist sentiment. Plays on figures like Kittur Channamma and Sangolli Rayanna kindled anti-British fervor, motivating more to join the Congress and creating an environment conducive to the nationalist movement.
Karachi Congess Session-1931: The Karachi Session of Congress in 1931, held from March 26-31, marked significant developments. The Gandhi-Irwin Pact was endorsed, despite public anger due to recent executions. Gandhi faced black flags on his way to the session. Congress dissociated from political violence, admired martyrs’ bravery, endorsed the Pact, and reiterated the goal of “Poorna Swaraj.” The session’s key resolution on Fundamental Rights and Economic Policy, drafted by Nehru, defined Swaraj’s meaning for common people. It included civil rights, universal adult franchise, education, workers’ rights, women’s protection, and state control of industries.

explanation:
Exp) Option c is the correct answer.
The Nehru Report was prepared by a committee headed by Motilal Nehru. The subject of the Nehru Report was “Constitutional arrangements in India” J.L. Nehru was acting as a secretary. There were 9 members in this committee. The final report was signed by M.L. Nehru and J.L. Nehru, Tej Bahadur Sapru, Ali Imam, Madhav Shrihari Aney, Shuaib Qureshi, Mangal Singh, Subhas Chandra Bose, and G. R. Pradhan. It was a significant document that outlined the proposed constitutional framework for India’s future governance and sought a dominion status for India within the British Commonwealth. The report addressed various aspects of governance, representation, and rights, and played a pivotal role in shaping discussions on India’s constitutional reforms.

Important Tips

Recommendations of Nehru Report:
Dominion Status and Parliamentary Government: Suggested granting India Dominion Status, featuring a parliamentary system of government. The legislature should be bicameral, consisting of a Senate and a House of Representatives.
Responsible Government: Advocated responsible government at both the central and provincial levels. The Governor-General and Governors should act on the advice of the executive councils, which would be collectively responsible to the legislature.
Federal Structure: Proposed a federal form of government, with residual powers vested in the central authority.
Provincial Councils: Suggested provincial councils with a 5-year term, headed by Governors who would act based on the advice of the provincial executive councils.

explanation:
Exp) Option b is the correct answer.
The Non-Cooperation Movement led by Mahatma Gandhi was halted due to the Chauri-Chaura incident. The Chauri Chaura incident was a violent protest that took place on February 4, 1922, in the town of Chauri Chaura in Gorakhpur district of Uttar Pradesh. A group of protesters clashed with police and set fire to a police station, killing 22 policemen. This incident shocked Mahatma Gandhi, who felt that the movement had become violent and that it was no longer following the principles of non-violence. He called off the movement on February 12, 1922.

Important Tips

Kakori Case: The Kakori Train Action occurred on 9 August 1925 near Lucknow during the Indian independence movement. Organized by Hindustan Republican Association (HRA) members like Ram Prasad Bismil and Ashfaqullah Khan, it aimed to fund anti-British activities. The train was stopped, British funds were looted, and one passenger was-unintentionally killed.The event brought attention to HRA’ cause.
The Jallianwala Bagh massacre: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre occurred on 13 April 1919 in Amritsar, British India. General Dyer surrounded a peaceful crowd protesting the Rowlatt Act and ordered his troops to open fire, killing at least 379 and injuring over 1,200. The brutal event sparked outrage, eroding Indian trust in British intentions and fueling the non-cooperation movement.
The Muzaffarpur Conspiracy Case: The Muzaffarpur Conspiracy Case (1908) revolved around the bomb attack on Chief Magistrate Douglas Kingsford’s carriage by Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki in Muzaffarpur, Bihar. Bose was arrested while Chaki committed suicide. The trial began on 21 May 1908 with Khudiram, Mrityunjay Chakraborty, and Kishorimohan Bandopadhyay. Despite his defense, Khudiram was sentenced to death at the age of 18 and faced the sentence with a smile.

Malabar Rebellion or Moplah Uprising or Mapillah Revolt (1921) was an offshoot of Khilafat agitation movement. The anti-British sentiment fuelled by these agitations affected the Muslim Mapillahs (also known as Moplahs) of south Malabar region of Kerala.

Important Tips

Malabar Rebellion or Moplah Uprising:

  • After the death of Tipu Sultan in 1799 in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War, Malabar had come under British authority as part of the Madras Presidency.
  • The British had introduced new tenancy laws that tremendously favoured the landlords known as Janmis and instituted a far more exploitative system for peasants than before.
  • The new laws deprived the peasants of all guaranteed rights to the land, share in the produce they earlier got and in effect rendered them landless.
  • Most of the landlords were Namboodiri Brahmins while most of the tenants were Mapillah Muslims.
  • Fuelled by the fiery speeches by Muslim religious leaders and anti-british sentiments, the Mopillahs launched a violent rebellion. Numerous actions of violence were reported, and series of persecutions were committed both against the British and the Hindu landlords.
  • By the end of 1921, the rebellion was crushed by the British who had raised a special battalion, the Malabar Special Force for the riot.
  • In November 1921, 67 Moplah prisoners were killed when they were being transported in a closed freight wagon from Tirur to the Central Prison in Podanur. They died of suffocation. This event is called the Wagon Tragedy.

The agitation against the Chaukidari Tax in Begusarai was a significant component of the Civil Disobedience Movement. As Bihar lacked access to the sea, the Salt Satyagraha, a prominent aspect of the movement, was not feasible here. Instead, the local residents initiated a campaign by refusing to pay the Chowkidari Tax, which was a levy imposed on farmers in 1907 to support village watchmen. This tax disproportionately burdened poorer farmers, prompting a revolt in 1930 as part of the civil disobedience movement, led by Swami Sahajanand Saraswati, a Hindu monk and social reformer. The movement achieved success in areas like Bhagalpur, Munger, and Saran, resulting in the dismissal of chowkidars and panchayat members responsible for their appointments. However, the British responded with a harsh crackdown, arresting and imprisoning many movement leaders, including Saraswati himself, who endured several years of incarceration.

Exp) Option a is the correct answer.
The Second Round Table Conference failed to reach an agreement on the issue of communal representation. The Indian National Congress wanted a system of joint electorates, where all Indians would vote for all seats, regardless of their religion. The Muslim League wanted a system of separate electorates, where Muslims would vote for Muslim seats and Hindus would vote for Hindu seats. The conference ended without any agreement being reached on the issue of communal representation. He was convinced by Fujiwara, a Japanese official, to unite with the Japanese mission for the purpose of Indian independence. Mohan Singh initially helped Fujiwara take control of the situation in Alor Star, and after meetings with Japanese officials, he was convinced of the feasibility of raising an armed Indian unit. This led to the formation of the nucleus of what became the Ajad Hind Fauj (Indian National Army) in 1942. Mohan Singh played a crucial role in recruiting Indian prisoners of war and volunteers to fight for India’s independence from British rule. While initially playing a significant role, leadership was later taken over by Subhash Chandra Bose.

Important Tips

Formation of INA:

  • During World War II, Indian revolutionary Rashbehari Bose, who had been living in Japan since 1915 to evade British authorities, saw an opportunity to mobilize Indians for armed resistance against British rule.
  • With numerous Indian soldiers serving the British, the Japanese, after defeating the British in Southeast Asia, convinced Captain Mohan Singh to collaborate with them for India’s freedom.
  • A conference in Tokyo in 1942 led to the formation of the Indian Independence League. Subsequently, in Bangkok (June 1942), Rashbehari Bose was elected its president, and the decision to establish the Indian National Army (INA) was made. Captain Mohan Singh became its commander with around 40,000 Indian soldiers.
  • Bose, who had earlier escaped to Berlin in 1941, was invited to lead the movement. In June 1943, Bose arrived in Tokyo and joined the INA in Singapore. Rashbehari Bose handed leadership to Subhas Bose, resulting in the formation of the Azad Hind Sarkar.
  • The Japanese later announced their pian to transfer administration of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands to the INA in November 1943. This marked the commencement of the INA’s valiant struggle for India’s independence.

Shimla Conference, June 1945: The Shimla Conference invited Indian leaders, including Gandhi and Jinnah, to discuss the Wavell Plan. Differences emerged as Jinnah insisted on exclusive Muslim League representation and veto power. The conference failed, leading to dissolution and the approach of Indian independence.
INA Trials, Nov 1945: INA Trials were held against Indian National Army (INA) officers who had fought against the British during World War II. The trials.were highly. controversial, and they ultimately led to the release of the INA officers.
Naval Mutiny, Feb 1946: This was a mutiny of Indian sailors in the Royal Indian Navy. The mutiny was triggered by a number of grievances, including low pay and poor living conditions. The mutiny was suppressed by the British, but it had a major impact on Indian politics.

  2. Withdraw of non-cooperation movement by Mahatma Gandhi.

explanation:

Statement 1 is correct: The Non-Cooperation Movement led by Mahatma Gandhi gained significant momentum but was abruptly withdrawn after the Chauri Chaura incident in 1922. Many leaders and activists felt demoralized by the withdrawal and believed that political engagement within the legislative councils was necessary to continue the struggle for self-rule.
Statement 2 is correct: The Government of India Act of 1919 introduced limited self-government in India through the formation of legislative councils. The Swaraj Party decided to enter these councils and use them as platforms to oppose repressive laws, inadequate representation, and to demand more powers for Indians in governance. While they participated, they also resisted and criticized the functioning of these councils.
Statement 3 is incorrect: While repression by the British Government might have played a role in shaping the context of political decisions, it is not a direct reason for the founding of the Swaraj Party. The party was formed to engage in legislative councils strategically rather than as a direct response to repression.
Statement 4 is incorrect: While there might have been some sentiment among Indians to gain experience in administration, it was not a primary reason for the founding of the Swaraj Party. The main focus was on utilizing the legislative councils as a platform to push for self-governance and political rights.

Important Tips

Works and Achievements of Swaraj Party:

  • Electoral Success: The Swarajists emerged as the largest party in the Central Assembly, Bombay, and Bengal Councils in 1923, with a notable presence in the U.P. Council.
  • Preserving Anti-British Sentiment: During a period with limited mass political activities, the Swarajists played a crucial role in maintaining the spirit of anti British protest.
  • Obstruction of British Policies: The Swarajists obstructed British policies and proposals in legislatures, making it challenging for the British to gain approval for their measures.
  • Defeat of Repressive Bills: Notably, in 1928, they defeated a bill that would have empowered the government to expel foreign supporters of India’s freedom struggle.
  • Exposing Reforms’ Weaknesses: They highlighted the shortcomings of the Montagu-Chelmsford reforms through fiery speeches in the Assembly, emphasizing self-rule and civil liberties.
  • Legislative Impact: The years 1924-25 saw numerous Swarajist victories in the Legislative Assembly. They managed to reject the Budget, compelling the government to rely on certification powers.
  • Questioning and Adjournment Motions: Swarajists effectively employed adjournment motions and probing questions to unveil the wrongdoings of the colonial government, exposing its misdeeds.

subject: Modern History
question: 1. Who among the following officers of Azad Hind Fauj did NOT face famous Red Fort trials?
explanation:
Exp) Option c is the correct answer.
The Indian National Army trials, also known as the Red Fort trials, were a series of court-martial proceedings conducted by the British Indian authorities between November 1945 and May 1946. These trials involved officers of the Indian National Army (INA) who fought for India’s independence alongside the Japanese during Worid War II. Colonel Prem Sahgal, Colonel Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon, and Major- General Shah Nawaz Khan faced charges of “waging war against the King-Emperor,” murder, and abetment of murder.
Mohan Singh did not face these trials. Mohan Singh was initially the leader of the INA, but in June 1943 he was replaced due to disagreements between him and the Japanese, over both the intended size and the specific role of the INA. Due to this leadership change and his subsequent lack of involvement with the INA’s actions under Bose’s leadership, he did not face the Red Fort trials.

Important Tips

Key Highlights of Red Fort Trials:

  • Initiated by British Indian authorities to prosecute INA officers.
  • Congress, led by Jawaharlal Nehru, accepted responsibility for the trials. A defense committee, including Nehru, Bhulabhai Desai, -Tej Bahadur Sapru and others, was formed to support INA soldiers.
  • Over 7,600 INA members initially faced trial, but the number was reduced due to evidentiary challenges.
  • About ten court-martials were conducted, with the first involving Prem Sahgal, Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon, and Shah Nawaz Khan. These officers had served in the British Indian Army and joined INA, facing charges of waging war against the King-Emperor, murder, and abetment.
  • Trials encompassed legal arguments in military, constitutional, and international law, becoming a notable anticolonial critique.
  • Lt. Col. Horilal Varma and Tej Bahadur Sapru defended the accused.
  • Public outcry and growing unrest led Field Marshal Claude Auchinleck to commute the sentences of the first trial’s defendants, symbolizing the trials’ impact on India’s independence movement.

question: 1. By a Regulation in 1793, the District Collector was deprived of his judicial powers and made the collecting agent only. What was the reason for such regulation?
options: Lord Cornwallis felt that the District Collector's efficiency of revenue collection would enormously increase without the burden of other work.
Lord Cornwallis felt that judicial power should compulsorily be in the hands of Europeans, while Indians can be given the job of revenue collection in the districts.
Lord Cornwallis was alarmed at the extent of power concentrated in the District Collector and felt that such absolute power was undesirable in one person.
The judicial work demanded a deep knowledge of India and a good training in law and Lord Cornwallis felt that District Collector should be only a revenue collector.
explanation:
The reason for such regulation was Lord Cornwallis was alarmed at the extent of power concentrated in the District Collector and felt that such absolute power was undesirable in one person. The revenue administration was separated from the judiciary functions by the Charter Act of 1793.

Important Tips

The features of Charter Act, 1793:

  • It gave the Governor-General more powers and control over the governments of the subordinate Presidencies of Bombay and Madras.
  • It extended the trade monopoly of the Company in India for another period of twenty years.
  • It stated that the Commander-in-Chief was not to be a member of the Governor-General’s council, unless he was so appointed.
  • The Home Government members were to be paid out of Indian revenues, which continued up to 1919.
  • The Company, after paying the necessary expenses, interest, dividends, salaries, etc., from the Indian revenues, was to pay 5 lakh pounds annually to the British government.
  • The royal approval was mandated for the appointment of the Governor General, the Governors, and the Commander-in-Chief.
  • Senior officials of the Company were debarred from leaving India without permission. Doing so was treated as resignation.

question: 1. Under the Permanent Settlement, 1793, the Zamindars were required to issue pattas to the farmer which were not issued by many of the Zamindars. The reason was:
options: the Zamindars were trusted by the farmers
there was no officials check upon the Zamindars
it was the responsibility of the British government
the farmers were not interested in getting pattas
explanation:
The zamindars were required to issue pattas to the farmers under the Permanent Settlement of 1793. However, many zamindars did not issue pattas to the farmers. The reason for this was that there was no official check upon the zamindars. The British government did not have the resources to monitor the zamindars effectively. As a result, the zamindars were able to exploit the farmers without fear of reprisal. The pattas were important for the farmers because they gave them a legal right to the land they were cultivating. Without pattas, the farmers were vulnerable to eviction by the zamindars. The zamindars often used the threat of eviction to extract more rent from the farmers.

Important Tips

Challenges of the Zamindari System:

  • Impact on Cultivators:
  • High Rents: Cultivators faced oppression and exploitation due to exorbitant rents charged by zamindars.
  • Land Insecurity: The uncertainty of land ownership under the system added to their woes.
  • Indebtedness: Many cultivators had to borrow money to pay rents, leading to cycles of debt.
  • Eviction Threat: Failure to pay rents resulted in eviction from the land, worsening their situation.
  • Struggles for Zamindars:
  • High Revenue: The fixed revenue demand was often challenging for zamindars to meet.
  • Risk of Loss: Zamindars failing to pay revenue risked losing their zamindari rights.
  • Lack of Incentive: Zamindars were more interested in collecting rents than investing in land improvement.
  • Limitations for the Company:
  • Growing Cultivation: Increased cultivation and rising prices benefited zamindars but not the colonial company.
  • Revenue Constraint: The company couldn't adjust the permanent revenue demand despite changing economic conditions.
  • Stagnant Income: The company’s income remained stagnant, even as agrarian activities expanded.
    Page 22

question: 1. The most short-lived of all of Britain’s constitutional experiments in India was:
explanation:
The most short-lived of all of Britain’s constitutional experiments in India was Indian Council Act of 1909. The Indian Councils Act of 1909 is also called Morley-Minto Reforms. It lasted only for 10 years until Government of India Act of 1919 was introduced.

Important Tips

The features of Indian Council Act, 1909:

  • It considerably increased the size of the legislative councils, both Central and provincial. The number of members in the Central legislative council was raised from 16 to 60. The number of members in the provincial legislative councils was not uniform.
  • The Act of 1909 created non-official majority of members in all the Provincial Legislative Councils, but maintained official majority of members in the Central Legislative Council.
  • It enlarged the deliberative functions of the legislative councils at both levels. For example, members were allowed to ask supplementary questions, move resolutions on the budget and so on.
  • For the first time, it provided for the association of Indians with the executive councils of the Viceroy and Governors. Satyendra Prasad Sinha became the first Indian to join the Viceroy’s executive council. He was appointed as the Law Member.
  • It also provided for the separate representation of presidency corporations, chambers of commerce, universities and zamindars.

explanation:
The Harcourt Butler Committee, chaired by Sir Harcourt Butler in 1923, clarified British paramountcy over princely states in India. It reaffirmed the doctrine of paramountcy, provided guidelines for its application, and emphasized fair financial dealings. Princely states wouldn't be transferred without their consent to Indian government control.

The Hartog Committee, formed in 1929 by the Simon Commission in British India and led by Philip Hartog, aimed to address issues in education. It prioritized mass education, identified problems in primary schools like wastage and stagnation, and recommended government oversight. It also suggested curriculum reforms for secondary and higher education, advocated for women’s education, and highlighted the need for improved facilities.

The Hunter Commission was established after the Jallianwala Bagh massacre in 1919. Led by Lord William Hunter, it found General Dyer’s actions unjustified, but justified martial law in Punjab. The majority report reprimanded Dyer for his duty concept, while the minority report questioned martial law’s necessity and disturbance severity. Compensation was provided to the victims’ dependents.

The Muddiman Committee, led by Sir Alexander Muddiman in 1924, addressed Indian leaders’ demands regarding the diarchy issue in the 1921 Indian Council Act. It produced majority and minority reports, with the majority suggesting minor changes, while the minority called for a permanent Constitution. Lord Birkenhead favored the majority report.

subject: Modern History
question: 1. Which one of the following statements correctly defines the term ‘Drain Theory’ as propounded by Dadabhai Naoroji?
options: That the resources of the country were being utilized in the interest of Britain.
That a part of Indians national wealth or total annual product was being exported to Britain for which India got no material returns.
That the British industrialists were being given an opportunity to invest in India under the protection of the imperial power.
That the British goods was being imported to the country making it miserable day by day.
explanation:
Drain Theory as propounded by Dadabhai Naoroji refers to the concept that a part of India’s national wealth or total annual product was being drained or exported to Britain without commensurate material returns to India. He calculated that India was losing about £150 million every year to Britain.

The drain theory was based on the following factors:

  • The excess of exports over imports, which meant that India was sending more goods to Britain than it was receiving from Britain.
  • The high salaries paid to British officials in India, which were then sent back to Britain.
  • The profits made by British companies in India, which were also sent back to Britain.
  • The cost of the British military in India, which was paid for by the Indian government.

Important Tips

Impacts of Wealth Drain from India:

  • Reduced Local Circulation of Money: Money sent abroad hindered local economic circulation, impacting trade, industries, and agriculture. This deprived local businesses and individuals of the benefits of circulating capital within India.
  • Stifled Economic Growth: The drain impeded the growth of vital sectors like trades, industries, and agriculture that relied on circulating capital. Capital outflow to England led to a shortage of funds, hindering substantial industrial development.
  • Impoverishment of Peasantry: Draining land revenue, a key capital source, led to rural impoverishment. The peasantry was disproportionately affected, denying them potential economic growth opportunities.
  • Capital Shortage and Industrial Stagnation: Loss of productive capital hindered India’s industrial growth, preventing robust manufacturing development. Capital scarcity impeded India’s own industrial revolution.
  • Inhibited Capital Formation: Drainage disrupted capital formation necessary for long-term economic growth, curtailing India’s potential for domestic development.
  • Skewed Socioeconomic Structure: The drain worsened wealth inequality, hindering middle-class formation and marginalizing socioeconomic progress.
  • Undermined Self-Reliance: Wealth drainage weakened India’s internal resource generation, heightening dependence on foreign capital.
    Page 23-24

subject: Modern History
question: 1. The foundation of the modern educational system in India was laid by:
explanation:
The foundation of the modern educational system in India was established by Macaulay’s Minutes of 1835. In this historic document, Thomas Babington Macaulay emphasized the importance of providing English education to Indians. He believed that this approach would create a class of Indians who shared British values and interests. This marked a significant shift in educational policy, promoting Western sciences and literature in English as the primary focus of education in India. This approach aimed to produce individuals who were “Indian in blood and color, but English in taste, opinions, morals, and intellect.”

Important Tips

The Macaulay Minute of 1835:
Objectives:

  • Exclusivity of Western Education: The famous Lord Macaulay’s Minute settled the dispute in favor of Anglicists—the limited government resources were to be devoted solely to the teaching of Western sciences and literature in English, excluding other forms of education.
  • University Closure: He advocated for the closure of universities offering courses solely in eastern philosophy.
  • Downward Filtration Theory: Macaulay suggested a limited number of Indians should receive government education, who would then disseminate knowledge to the broader population, known as the “downward filtration” approach.
  • Indian-British Identity: His vision aimed to cultivate Indians who could align with British interests—being “Indian by blood and colour, but English by likes, beliefs, morality, and intellect”
    Features:
  • Promotion of European Education: Macaulay stressed the importance of emphasizing European science and literature for Indians, suggesting that resources be allocated primarily to English education.
  • Stipends and Education: New students entering institutions under the committee would not receive stipends. However, existing professors and students would continue to be stipend recipients.
  • Oriental Works Funding: Government funds would no longer support the publication of oriental works.
  • Future Allocation: Macaulay’s proposal directed future government expenditures exclusively to English literature and science education for Indians.
    Page 24

explanation:
When debate on the inclusion of separate electorate in Indian Constitution was conducted, Sardar Vallabh Bhai Patel said in constituent assembly, “Can you show me one free country where there are separate electorates? ..... 1. Given below are two statements, one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R):
    Assertion (A): The British Government introduced different land revenue system in different part of India.
    Reason (R): It led to create different classes in India peasantry.

Select the correct answer from the codes given below.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
explanation:
Assertion (A) is true: The British Government did introduce different land revenue systems in various parts of India based on local conditions, historical practices, and economic considerations. For instance, the Permanent Settlement, Ryotwari System, and Mahalwari System were implemented in different regions.

Reason (R) is true: The introduction of varied land revenue systems did lead to the emergence of different classes among the peasantry, depending on how the systems operated and the rights granted to landholders. The systems affected landownership, tenancy, and economic relationships differently across regions.

Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A): While it’s true that the introduction of different land revenue systems resulted in the creation of different classes within the Indian peasantry, the connection between the two statements is not as straightforward as cause and effect. The creation of different classes was not the purpose of introducing different revenue systems; rather, it was a consequence of a complex set of factors including administrative policies, economic considerations, and social dynamics.

Important Tips

  • The jajmani system, prevalent mainly in North India, was an economic arrangement where some castes provided specific services to other castes in return for goods, maintaining a patron-client relationship. Services were hereditary, exchanged within families, fostering self-sufficient village economies.
  • The Bara Balutedar system in Maharashtra comprised twelve hereditary trades with roles like priests, barbers, blacksmiths, and more. They received village produce for services under a barter system. Balutedars held privileges at ceremonies and received payments in cash or kind. This system, akin to the jajmani system, was agriculturally linked and had hereditary rights. It was abolished by law in 1958.
  • In pre-colonial South India, land was intertwined with social relationships, forming a ‘share distribution system.’ Village produce was divided into shares, sustaining those in production roles. The mirasi system, analogous to inherited rights, prevailed, fostering flexibility by linking shares to roles, accommodating mobility. Temples and Brahmins also received dues. This indigenous, enduring mirasi system played a pivotal role in Tamil Nadu’s history.

question:
1. Arrange the following events in their chronological order and select the correct answer from the codes given below:
    A. Hunter Commission
    B. Sadlar Commission
    C. Wood’s Despatch
    D. Sargeant Plan
explanation:
The correct chronological order of the events is as follows:

  • Wood’s Despatch (1854): Charles Wood, President of the Board of Control of the East India Company, sent the influential Wood’s Despatch in 1854 to Lord Dalhousie, promoting English education in India with vernacular languages in primary schools and English as the medium in colleges, shaping Indian education significantly.
  • Hunter Commission (1882): The Hunter Commission of 1882 made several key recommendations for the education system in British India, including: prioritizing literate candidates for government jobs, expanding primary schools in underdeveloped areas, entrusting local self-government bodies with primary education management, encouraging private secondary schools with government funds, revising the secondary school curriculum, discouraging missionary schools, and promoting the education of girls and women.
  • Sadler Commission (1917): The Sadler Commission of 1917, also known as the Calcutta University Commission, was established to address issues in Calcutta University and Indian education. It recommended improvements in teacher training, university autonomy, separation of secondary and university education, and the establishment of boards for secondary and intermediate education. It also emphasized the need for women’s education and the expansion of educational institutions in towns.
  • Sargeant Plan (1944): The Sergeant Plan of Education, outlined in the 1944 Sargent Report, proposed a comprehensive educational system with pre-primary education for 3-6-year-olds, universal primary education for ages 6-11 and 11-14, middle schools with diverse courses, and high schools divided into academic and technical streams. It emphasized mother tongue instruction, teacher training, physical education, and equal opportunities for students.

1. Consider the following statements and select the correct answer from the code given below the statements:
    Assertion (A): Generally, India had a favourable balance of trade during the British rule.
    Reason (R): The drain of wealth took the form of unrequired exports.

Code:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
explanation:
Assertion (A) is true: India did generally have a favorable balance of trade during British rule. It implies that the value of its exports exceeded the value of its imports, resulting in a surplus. This was due to the significant export of raw materials, agricultural products, and handicrafts from India to Britain.

Reason (R) is true: The drain of wealth from India took the form of unrequired exports, where valuable resources and goods were exported to Britain without receiving proportionate benefits in return. This economic exploitation led to a significant outflow of wealth from India, contributing to its economic subjugation.

(R) is the correct explanation of (A): The drain of wealth, characterized by unrequired exports, played a crucial role in maintaining the favorable balance of trade for Britain. India’s surplus exports contributed to Britain's economic prosperity while hindering India’s own development. Thus, the drain of wealth was the underlying reason behind India’s favorable trade balance during British rule.

question: 1. Which of the following is one of the reasons for considering the Charter Act of 1813 important for India?
options: It banned propaganda by Christian Missionaries in India.
It made a financial allocation for the education of Indian people.
It approved the development of a railway system in India.
explanation:
One of the reasons for considering the Charter Act of 1813 important for India is it made a financial allocation for the education of Indian people. It provided for the spread of western education among the inhabitants of the British territories in India. A sum of one lakh rupees was to be set aside for the revival, promotion, and encouragement of literature, learning, and science among the natives of India, every year.

Important Tips

The features of Charter Act, 1813:

  • It abolished the trade monopoly of the company in India i.e., the Indian trade was thrown open to all British merchants. However, it continued the monopoly of the company over trade in tea and trade with China.
  • It allowed the Christian missionaries to come to India for the purpose of enlightening the people.
  • It authorised the Local Governments in India to impose taxes on persons. They could also punish the people for not paying taxes.
  • The regulations made by the Councils of Madras, Bombay, and Calcutta were now required to be laid before the British Parliament. The constitutional position of the British territories in India was thus explicitly defined for the first time.

subject: Modern History
question: 1. Which of the following Acts for the first time created a functioning Legislature Council in India?
explanation:
Charter Act of 1853 for the first time created a functioning Legislature Council in India. It separated, for the first time, the legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General’s council. It established a separate Governor-General’s legislative council which came to be known as the Indian (Central) Legislative Council. This legislative wing of the council functioned as a mini-Parliament, adopting the same procedures as the British Parliament. Thus, for the first-time legislation was treated as a special function of the government.

Important Tips

The features of Charter Act, 1853:

  • It introduced an open competition system of selection and recruitment of civil servants. The covenanted civil service was, thus, thrown open to the Indians also.
  • It introduced, for the first time, local representation in the Indian (Central) Legislative Council. Of the six new legislative members of the Governor General’s council, four members were appointed by the local (provincial) governments of Madras, Bombay, Bengal and Agra.
  • The Charter Act of 1853 stated that the Company would be responsible for paying the salaries of the Board of Control members, its secretary, and other officers.
  • The Court of Directors, by the Act, also could alter the boundaries of the existing states and incorporate the newly acquired state.
  • Power was given to the Court of Directors to constitute a new Presidency.

subject: Modern History
question: 1. By which of the following Acts, the British for the first time introduced the system of indirect elections in India?
explanation:
Under Indian Councils Act of 1892, the British for the first time introduced the system of indirect elections in India. The act brought the provision of bringing additional members into the Legislative Council through the indirect election. For the first time, the element of an election was introduced into the Indian political system.

Important Tips

The features of Indian Councils Act, 1892:

  • It increased the number of additional (non-official) members in the Central and provincial legislative councils but maintained the official majority in them.
  • It increased the functions of legislative councils and gave them the power of discussing the budget and addressing questions to the executive.
  • The act made a limited and indirect provision for the use of election in filling up some of the non-official seats both in the Central and provincial legislative councils. The word “election” was, however, not used in the Act.

subject: Modern History
question: 1. The Indian Famine Code, 1883 was prepared by:
explanation:
The Indian Famine Code of 1883 was prepared by the Strachey Commission. This commission, led by Richard Strachey, was appointed in 1880 by Lord Lytton, the then Viceroy of India, to formulate general principles and suggest measures for dealing with famines in India. The code recommended various measures, including adjusting wages for laborers, providing gratuitous relief to the poor, and suspensions/remissions of land revenue and rents during famine situations. It also laid the foundation for the provincial famine codes.

Important Tips

Other Famine Commission:

  • Campbell Commission, 1866:
  • Famine in Odisha, Bengal, Bihar, and Madras in 1865-66.
  • 20 lakhs lives lost, with Odisha alone witnessing 10 lakhs casualties.
  • Committee led by Sir George Campbell.
  • Blamed government machinery for the tragedy.
  • Viceroy Sir John Lawrence in office.
  • Lyall Commission, 1896:
  • Famine of 1896-97 affecting nearly every province, impacting 34 million people.
  • Sir James Lyall chaired the commission.
  • Recommended flexibility to existing principles.
  • Advocated the development of irrigation facilities.
  • Lord Elgin II was the Viceroy.
  • McDonnell Commission, 1900:
  • Led by MacDonnell.
  • Stressed moral strategy, early distribution of advances for agriculture, and sinking temporary wells.
  • Recommended the appointment of a famine commissioner in provinces expecting extensive relief operations.
  • Emphasized non-official assistance, improved transport, agricultural banks, irrigation, and agricultural methods.
  • Many recommendations accepted, but some measures implemented half-heartedly under Lord Curzon’s administration.

subject: Modern History
question: 1. In whose reign was English Education introduced in India
explanation:
English education was introduced in India in the reign of Lord William Cavendish Bentinck, who was the Governor-General of India from 1828 to 1835. Bentinck was a strong advocate of Western education, and he believed that it was essential for the modernization of India. In 1835, he passed the English Education Act, which made English the medium of instruction in all government schools. This act marked the beginning of the spread of English education in India.

Important Tips

Feature of The English Education Act of 1835:

  • Legislative Implementation: Enacted by the Council of India, the Act enforced a decision by Lord William Bentinck to reallocate funds as mandated by the British Parliament for education and literature in India.
  • Shift in Support: Formerly, limited backing was given to traditional Muslim and Hindu education as well as literature in Sanskrit and Persian. The Act redirected support towards institutions teaching a Western curriculum with English as the medium of instruction.
  • Impact on Language: Alongside other measures promoting English in administration and law courts, the Act contributed to English becoming one of India’s languages, transcending its status as merely the language of foreign rulers. English became the language of the Higher Education in India.
  • Macaulay’s Memorandum: Thomas Babington Macaulay’s influential Memorandum on (Indian) Education, a catalyst for the Act, emphasized Western superiority and proposed English-medium higher education to produce individuals “Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste, opinions, morals, and intellect”
  • Hybrid Approach: While Macaulay’s memorandum advocated reduced support for traditional education, the Act exhibited a more balanced stance and led to subsequent funding provisions for both traditional and Western education.
  • Vernacular Language: Vernacular language education received limited funding under the Act, despite historical underrepresentation.
    Page 30
questionText: In whose reign was English Education introduced in India

explanation:
The Permanent Settlement was introduced by Lord Cornwallis in 1793. It was a system of land revenue settlement in Bengal and Bihar. Under the Permanent Settlement, the zamindars were given the right to collect land revenue from the peasants in return for a fixed annual payment to the British government. The Permanent Settlement was intended to create a stable and reliable source of revenue for the British government and to encourage the zamindars to invest in agriculture.

Important Tips

The Permanent Settlement Agreement:

  • The Permanent Settlement Agreement established the Zamindars as permanent landowners.
  • Under this arrangement, Zamindars were obligated to remit 89% of the annual revenue to the state while retaining 11% as their portion. Also, the revenue was fixed at 89% of the production of 1779-80.
  • This settlement also granted Zamindars autonomy over the internal affairs within their districts.

subject: Modern History
question: 1. Who among the following introduced the Vernacular Press Act?
explanation:
Lord Lytton introduced the Vernacular Press Act to prevent newspapers from printing ‘seditious material’. The European press used to publish content in favour of the British government whereas the vernacular press was critical of the government. The Vernacular Press Act (VPA) of 1878 was designed to ‘better control’ the vernacular press and effectively punish and repress “seditious writing” in publications in oriental languages (Indian languages). The act came to be nicknamed “the gagging Act”.

Important Tips

The provisions of the Vernacular Press Act, 1878:

  • The district magistrate was empowered to call upon the printer and publisher of any vernacular newspaper to enter into a bond with the government.
  • The printer and publisher could also be required to deposit security, which could be forefeited if the regulations were contravened, and press equipment could be seized if the offence re-occurred.
  • The magistrate’s action was final and no appeal could be made in a court of law.
  • A vernacular newspaper could get exemption from the operation of the act by submitting proofs to a government censor.
    The worst features of this act were:
  • Discrimination between English and vernacular press.
  • No right of appeal.
    Page 31

question: 1. In the Hunter Commission report, special emphasis was laid on the development of:
explanation:
In the Hunter Commission report of 1882, special emphasis was placed on the development of primary education in India. The commission, chaired by W.W. Hunter, reviewed the educational progress in the country and recommended measures to improve primary education. The commission’s focus was on assessing the state of primary education and making recommendations for its extension and enhancement. The commission argued that primary education was essential for the overall development of the country and that it would help to improve the lives of the people.

Important Tips

The Hunter Commission of 1882 made significant recommendations that led to key changes in British India’s education system:

  • Mother Tongue as Medium: Primary education should use the mother tongue as the medium of instruction.
  • Enhanced Teacher Training: Increased establishment of training schools for the proper training of primary teachers.
  • Model Government High School: Creation of model government high schools was suggested.
  • Practical and Localized Curriculum: The school curriculum should prioritize practical aspects and cater to local needs.
  • Local Self-Government Involvement: Primary education management was entrusted to district and municipal boards under the Local Self Government Act. Separate funds were allocated for rural and urban areas to ensure proper allocation.
  • Promotion of Indian Participation: Missionary schools were discouraged, encouraging Indian engagement in private schools.
  • Addressing Female Education: Recognizing inadequate female education outside major cities, the commission urged the expansion of facilities for women’s education and put forth recommendations for its improvement.
  • Private Secondary Schools: Private entities were encouraged to establish secondary schools with government funding. Government-operated model schools in each district were suggested to guide these private institutions.
    Page 32

question: 1. Who authored the book “Poverty and the Unbritish Rule in India”?
explanation:
Dadabhai Naoroji, authored the book “Poverty and Un-British Rule in India” in 1901. The book presented his theory of wealth drain, revealing how resources were systematically transferred from India to Britain. Naoroji emphasized economic exploitation by detailing mechanisms like excessive exports, over-employment of British officials, and interest payments. His work fueled nationalist sentiment and the demand for self-governance.

Important Tips

Indian leaders provided varying estimates of the drain’s magnitude, subject to individual and yearly fluctuations:

  • R.C. Dutt: Around £20 million, half of India’s net revenue, was drained out annually in the early 20th century.
  • M.G. Ranade: More than one-third of India’s national income was taken by the government through various means.
  • Dadabhai Naoroji: Roughly one-fourth of India’s raised funds, approximately $12 million annually, flowed to England.
  • William Digby: His calculations suggested an annual drainage of £30 million.

explanation:

This system was established in British territories of southern India, where farmers directly paid land revenue to the state. Munro, along with Captain Alexander Read, devised this approach in the late 18th century, and Munro implemented it during his governorship of Madras Presidency from 1819 to 1826.

  • Named after individual cultivators called “ryots,” it granted them complete land rights, including sale and lease. Ryots, ensuring rent payment, couldn't be evicted.
