question: 1. The Indian Council Act of 1909 was provided for:
explanation:
The Indian Councils Act of 1909 introduced a system of communal representation for Muslims by accepting the concept of ‘separate electorate’. Under this, the Muslim members were to be elected only by Muslim voters.

Important Tips

Provisions of the Morley-Minto reforms:

  • The legislative councils at the Centre and the provinces increased in size.
  • The legislative councils at the Centre and the provinces were to have four categories of members as follows:
  • Ex officio members: Governor-General and members of the executive council.
  • Nominated official members: Government officials who were nominated by the Governor-General.
  • Nominated non-official members: nominated by the Governor-General but were not government officials.
  • Elected members: elected by different categories of Indians. The elected members were elected indirectly. The elected members were from the local bodies, the chambers of commerce, landlords, universities, traders’ communities and Muslims.
  • In the provincial councils, non-official members were in the majority. However, since some of the non-official members were nominated, in total, a non-elected majority was there.
  • Indians were given membership to the Imperial Legislative Council for the first time.
  • The members could discuss the budget and move resolutions. They could also discuss matters of public interest.
  • They could also ask supplementary questions.
  • No discussions on foreign policy or on relations with the princely states were permitted.

End of the Princely States by this
explanation:
The Government of India Act, 1935 is the main source of the Indian Constitution. The structural part of the Indian Constitution is, to a large extent, derived from the Government of India Act of 1935. About 250 provisions of the 1935 Act have been included in the Indian Constitution.

Important Tips

The features of Government of India Act, 1935:

  • It provided for the establishment of an All-India Federation consisting of provinces and princely states as units.
  • It abolished dyarchy in the provinces and introduced ‘provincial autonomy’ in its place.
  • It provided for the adoption of dyarchy at the Centre. Consequently, the federal subjects were divided into reserved subjects and transferred subjects.
  • It introduced bicameralism in six out of eleven provinces
  • It further extended the principle of communal representation by providing separate electorates for depressed classes (Scheduled Castes), women and labour (workers).
  • It abolished the Council of India, established by the Government of India Act of 1858. The secretary of state for India was provided with a team of advisors.
  • It extended franchise. About 10 per cent of the total population got the voting right.
  • It provided for the establishment of a Reserve Bank of India to control the currency and credit of the country.
  • It provided for the establishment of not only a Federal Public Service Commission, but also a Provincial Public Service Commission and Joint Public Service Commission for two or more provinces.
  • It provided for the establishment of a Federal Court, which was set up in 1937.
    Page 34-35

subject: Modern History
question: 1. Sadler Commission was related to:
explanation:
The Sadler Commission, also known as the Calcutta University Commission, was related to education. It was established in 1917 under the chairmanship of M.E. Sadler, the vice-chancellor of Leeds University. The commission was formed to inspect and address the challenges faced by Calcutta University, but its findings and recommendations had a significant impact on the overall education system in India. The commission highlighted issues related to university, secondary, and collegiate education and provided recommendations for improvement.

Important Tips

The 1917 Saddler Commission presented the following recommendations:

  • Teacher Training: Emphasis on teacher training and provision of adequate facilities for this purpose.
  • University Autonomy: Universities should function independently without external government control.
  • Intermediate Colleges: A distinction between secondary courses and university education was established. The government gained authority to establish Intermediate colleges.
  • Separate Boards: Different boards were formed for Intermediate and Secondary education.
  • Residential Teaching College: A separate residential teaching college was suggested in Dacca.
  • Vice-Chancellor Appointment: A full-time, paid Vice-Chancellor was to be appointed for administrative purposes.
  • Streamlined Curriculum: Intermediate Colleges should offer varied streams like Arts, Engineering, Science, and Industrial education.
  • Entry Criteria: Only students passing the intermediate examination, not just the Matriculation Examination, should be eligible for university admission.
  • Course Differentiation: Differentiation between Pass and Honours courses in university education.
  • Board Establishment: A Board of Secondary and Intermediate Education with representation from schools, government, universities, and Intermediate Colleges should be established.
  • Flexibility in Rules: Universities should have flexibility in framing rules and regulations.
  • Women’s Education: Establishment of a Board of Women Education at Calcutta University to promote women’s education.
    Page 35

question: 1. Identify the incorrect statement about Government of India Act 1919:
options: This Act is also known as Morley-Minto Reforms Act.
This Act separated the Central and Provincial subjects.
The Government of India Act 1919 came into force in 1921.
Montague was the Secretary of State for India and Lord Chelmsford was the Viceroy of India during Government of India Act 1919.
explanation:
The Indian Councils Act, 1909 (not Government of India Act 1919) is also known as Morley-Minto Reforms Act. Government of India Act, 1919 is known as Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms. Government of India Act 1919 separated the Central and Provincial subjects. The Government of India Act 1919 came into force in 1921. Montague was the Secretary of State for India and Lord Chelmsford was the Viceroy of India during Government of India Act 1919.

Important Tips

The features of Government of India Act, 1919:

  • It relaxed the central control over the provinces by demarcating and separating the central and provincial subjects.
  • It further divided the provincial subjects into two parts- transferred and reserved. The transferred subjects were to be administered by the Governor with the aid of Ministers responsible to the legislative council. The reserved subjects, on the other hand, were to be administered by the Governor and his executive council without being responsible to the legislative council. This dual scheme of governance was known as ‘dyarchy’.
  • It introduced, for the first time, bicameralism and direct elections in the country. Thus, the Indian legislative council was replaced by a bicameral legislature consisting of an Upper House (Council of State) and a Lower House (Legislative Assembly). The majority of members of both the Houses were chosen by direct election.
  • It required that the three of the six members of the Viceroy’s executive Council (other than the Commander-in-Chief) were to be Indian.
  • It extended the principle of communal representation by providing separate electorates for Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans.
  • It granted franchise to a limited number of people on the basis of property, tax or education.
  • It provided for the establishment of a public service commission. Hence, a Central Public Service Commission was set up in 1926 to recruit civil servants.
  • It separated, for the first time, provincial budgets from the Central budget and authorised the provincial legislatures to enact their budgets.
    Page 36-37

question: 1. The first three universities in India (Calcutta, Madras, and Bombay) were established in which year?
explanation:
The first three universities in India, namely Calcutta, Madras, and Bombay, were established in the year 1857. This development was a response to the Sir Charles Wood's Dispatch of 1854. These universities were founded to implement educational reforms and provide higher education in India.

Important Tips

Wood’s Despatch, 1854 recommendations:

  • Provincial Departments: The Despatch suggested creating Department of Public Instruction in the Provinces: Bombay, Madras, Punjab, and North-Western provinces.
  • Mass Education Expansion: Addressing limited opportunities, the Despatch stressed increasing primary, middle, and high schools for wider access to education.
  • University Establishment: It proposed universities in Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras, modeled after London University, encompassing subjects like Arabic, Sanskrit, Persian, law, and civil engineering.
  • Grant-in-Aid System: Advocating financial aid, the Despatch supported a grant-in-aid system for Indian education.
  • Language Emphasis: The Despatch emphasized teaching English while recognizing the significance of teaching Indian languages.
  • Women’s Education: It recommended government support for women’s education.
  • Teacher Training: Teacher training schools were suggested in each province, with specialized schools for engineering, medicine, and law instructors.
  • Graded School Network: The Despatch advocated establishing a nation-wide network of graded schools.

question: 1. The main reason for the British Government to spread modern education in India during the pre-independence period was-
options: The need for educated Indians in minor administrative posts
To modernize the Indian people so that they could share their political responsibilities
explanation:
The British Government’s primary motive behind promoting modern education in India was to address the challenge of staffing minor administrative positions. Given the logistical and financial difficulties of importing a sufficient number of English officials, they opted to train Indians in modern education to fill these administrative roles.

Important Tips

Other significant reasons for the British Government’s push for modern education:

  • Cultural Influence: The promotion of Western culture and values through education aimed to reshape Indian society according to British ideals, fostering a more interconnected colonial relationship.
  • Loyalty to British Rule: By educating a class of Indians in modern subjects, the British sought to create a segment of the population that was more aligned with and loyal to the British Raj, further solidifying their control over India.
  • Economic Development: The British anticipated that providing modern education to Indians would contribute to the development of the Indian economy by equipping individuals with skills relevant to emerging industries and trades.
    While these secondary reasons played a role, the fundamental objective of addressing the shortage of educated personnel for administrative roles remained the primary driver for the widespread promotion of modern education by the British Government in India.

Land bonds could not be executed by moneylenders

This meant that if a moneylender did not recover his loan within three years, he would lose the right to collect the debt.

  • The Limitation Law of 1859 was repealed in 1963 and replaced by the Limitation Act of 1963.
  • The new Act has a number of provisions that are designed to protect ryots from exploitation by moneylenders. For example, the Act stipulates that the maximum rate of interest that can be charged on a loan is 18%.

Statement 1 is correct- The Permanent Settlement was introduced by Lord Cornwallis during his tenure as the Governor-General of Bengal. The Ryotwari system involved direct settlement of land revenue with individual peasants (ryots) who were recognized as the cultivators and became the owners of their land. It was implemented in areas such as Madras Presidency, Bombay Presidency and some parts of Central Provinces.

Statement 3 is correct- The Mahalwari Settlement was introduced by Holt Mackenzie, a British administrator who served as the Governor of the North-Western Provinces during the early 19th century. The Mahalwari system involved the settlement of land revenue with village communities (mahals) collectively, where the village was treated as the unit of revenue assessment and collection. It was implemented in areas such as Punjab, North-Western Provinces, parts of Bihar, and some parts of Central Provinces.

subject: Modern History
question: 1. In 1902, Lord Curzon appointed the University Commission including two Indian members. Who were they?
explanation:
The University Commission appointed in 1902 by Lord Curzon aimed to recommend reforms in university education in India. The commission, led by Law member Thomas Raleigh, included two Indian members: Syed Hussain Bilgrami and Justice Gurudas Banerjee. Their recommendations covered a wide range of topics, including reformation of University Senates, greater representation of affiliated colleges, stricter monitoring of affiliated institutions, curricular reforms, education and examinations, research, student welfare, and state scholarships. These recommendations led to the enactment of the Indian Universities Act 1904, despite strong opposition from certain quarters in India.

Important Tips

The Indian Universities Act of 1904;

  • Autonomy and Activities: Universities gained the authority to conduct private teaching and other activities. They were responsible for teaching and examination supervision. Focus on research was emphasized, leading to the establishment of laboratories across disciplines.
  • Staff and Resources: Universities were empowered to hire new staff, recruit professionals, and establish libraries. This aimed to enrich students’ knowledge and learning experience.
  • Fellowships: The Act reduced the number of fellows from 100 to 50. Universities with more than 50 fellows faced greater accountability. Fellowships were limited to a six-month term instead of a lifetime.
  • Senate Election: Senate elections were introduced, with 20 elected fellows for Madras, Bombay, and Calcutta universities, and 15 for others. The government could intervene if the senate failed to formulate rules.
  • Syndicates and Representation: The Act recognized Syndicates in the education system. All university teachers gained representation in the university Senate.
  • Affiliation: Colleges needed affiliation with a specific university, which might not be within the local area’s jurisdiction. This aimed to strengthen the connection between colleges and universities.
  • Research Grants: INR 5 lakhs were allocated over five years to fellows for further studies and research.
  • Governor-General Council: The Act empowered the Governor-General Council to handle jurisdictional matters related to universities and their territories.
    Impact:
  • Criticism: The Sadler Commission (1917) criticized the Act for increasing governmental control over universities.
  • Nationalist Reaction: Nationalists saw the Act as reinforcing imperialism and suppressing nationalist sentiments. Gopal Krishna Gokhale labeled it a “retrograde measure.”
  • Primary Education: Lord Curzon used the Act’s reforms to enhance primary education, allocating substantial financial aid to schools between 1905 and 1912.
    Page 46

question: 1. The song ‘Amar Sonar Bangla’ written during the Swadeshi Movement of India inspired the liberation struggle of Bangladesh and was adopted as the National Anthem of Bangladesh. Who wrote this song? [UPSC CSE Pre 2007]
explanation:
Exp) Option d is the correct answer.
The song “Amar Sonar Bangla” was written by Rabindranath Tagore in 1905 during the first partition of Bengal, which occurred under British rule. The song served as an ode to Mother Bengal and was intended to rekindle the spirit of unity in Bengal amidst communal divisions. In 1971, during the liberation war of Bangladesh, the first ten lines of this song were adopted as the national anthem of Bangladesh, symbolizing its struggle for independence and the nation’s identity.

Important Tips

Rabindranath Tagore Literary works:
His poetic journey encompasses several remarkable collections, including “Manasi” (1890), known as “The Ideal One,” and “Sonar Tari” (1894), transiated as “The Golden Boat.” However, it was “Gitanjali” (1910), or “Song Offerings,” that catapulted him to international acclaim, earning him the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913. Tagore continued to enchant readers with “Gitimalya” (1914) and “Balaka” (1916), commonly referred to as “The Flight of Cranes.”
Tagore’s literary legacy extends into the realm of drama, with notable plays like “Raja” (1910), exploring themes of love and darkness, and “Dakghar” (1912), which poignantly captures the imagination of a young boy confined to his home. “Achalayatan” (1912) delves into the human spirit’s quest for freedom, while “Muktadhara” (1922) addresses societal reform. “Raktakaravi” (1926), or “Red Oleanders,” confronts themes of oppression and rebellion.
In addition to his dramatic works, Tagore ventured into prose and novels. “Gora” (1910) grapples with identity, social reform, and nationalism, while “Ghare-Baire” (1916), known as “The Home and the World,” delves into the complexities of love, politics, and personal ideals. “Yogayog” (1929), or “Crosscurrents,” explores the clash between tradition and modernity.
Beyond fiction, Tagore crafted an extensive body of work, including short stories, essays, travel diaries, and autobiographies. His creative talents extended to musical and dance dramas, and he was an accomplished artist, creating drawings and paintings.

explanation:

Vande Mataram is a poem written in Sanskrit and Sanskritised Bengali by Bankim Chandra Chatterjee in the 1870s. The first two verses of the poem were adopted as the National Song of India in October 1937 by the Congress. The poem was first published in 1882 as part of Chatterjee’s Bengali novel Anandmath. It is an ode to the motherland, personified as the “mother goddess” in later verses, of the people.

Important Tips

  • The National Calendar of India, following the Saka era, marks its first day of Chaitra on March 22 in regular years and on March 21 in leap years. This system was officially adopted on March 22, 1957, alongside the Gregorian calendar, for official purposes including Gazette publications, All India Radio broadcasts, Government-issued calendars, and public communications.
  • The national flag of India is a horizontal rectangular tricolour flag, the colours being of India saffron, white and India green; with the Ashoka Chakra, a 24-spoke wheel, in navy blue at its centre. It was adopted in its present form during a meeting of the Constituent Assembly held on 22 July 1947, and it became the official flag of the Union of India on 15 August 1947, The National Flag of India was designed by Pingali Venkayya in 1921.
  • “Jana Gana Mana” is the national anthem of the Republic of India. It was originally composed as Bharoto Bhagyo Bidhata in Bengali by Rabindranath Tagore on 11 December 1911, The first stanza of the song Bharoto Bhagyo Bidhata was adopted by the Constituent Assembly of India as the National Anthem on 24 January 1950. A formal rendition of the national anthem takes approximately 52 seconds. It was first publicly sung on 27 December 1911 at the Calcutta Session of the Indian National Congress.

question: 1. With reference to the Indian freedom struggle, which one of the following statements is not correct? [UPSC CSE Pre 2002]
options: Hakim Ajmal Khan was one of the leaders to start a nationalist and militant Ahrar movement.

The All-India Muslim League which was formed in 1906 vehemently opposed the partition of Bengal and separate electorates .

explanation:
Exp) Option c is the correct answer.
Sir syed Ahmed Khan felt that the Indian National Congress did not work towards the uplifment of the Indian Muslim community. Therefore, he opposed the Indian National Congress. Hence Statement b is correct.
A group of Muslim landlords and nawabs formed the All India Muslim League at Dacca in 1906. The League supported the partition of Bengal. It desired separate electorates for Muslims, a demand conceded by the government in 1909. Hence Statement c is not correct.
The Ahrar Movement was founded in 1910 under the leadership of Maulana Muhammad Ali Mohamed and Hakim Ajmal Khan. Other leaders of the movement were Iqbal, CR Das, Sir Mian Muhammad Shafi etc. These leaders were strictly against the Lucknow pact, which favoured the representation of religious minorities in provincial legislatures. The first Provisional Government of India was established in Kabul during First World War in December 1915. question: 1. Who among the following was the President of the All-India States Peoples Conference in 1939? [UPSC CSE Pre 2001]
explanation:
Exp) Option b is the correct answer
The 1939 Session of All India States People’s Conference was held at Ludhiana, Punjab under the leadership of Jawaharlal Nehru. Jawaharlal Nehru continued to hold this position till 1946. In his presidential speech to the Conference, titled “Freedom is Indivisible”, he denounced the political backwardness and oppression inflicted on the people. He also asserted the INC’s commitment to a united and free India, and criticized those who dreamt of political independence for their states separate from India. The Ludhiana Session of the All India States Peoples’ Conference was a milestone in the growth of the freedom movement, and signaled the unification of the different strands of nationalism that had developed.

Important Tips

The All India States Peoples’ Conference (AISPC) was the association of the Praja Mandals in the princely states under the British Raj. These Praja Mandals, established all over the country sought to introduce responsible government, accountable to people rather than being under absolute rule of local princes.
The first session of AISPC was held in Bombay in 1927 which brought together representatives from various Indian princely states.
In 1939, The Indian National Congress amended its policy to lend support to the AISPC.

question: 1. The last major extension of British Indian territory took place during the time of: [UPSC CSE Pre 2000]
explanation:
Exp) Option b is the correct answer.
Lord Dalhousie was the Governor-General of India from 1848 to 1856, and he was responsible for the last major extension of British Indian territory. He annexed many Indian states using the Doctrine of Lapse, which stated that if a ruler of a dependent state died without a natural heir, the state would be annexed by the British. Some of the states that were annexed by this policy were Jhansi, Satara, Jaitpur, Sambalpur, Udaipur, and Nagpur. He also annexed Awadh on the basis of misgovernance, accusing the Nawab of neglecting his subjects and failing to pay his debts to the British.
Lord Dalhousie’s aggressive expansionism and interference in the affairs of the Indian princes provoked resentment and resistance among the Indians, and contributed to the outbreak of the Indian Rebellion of 1857, which was also known as the First War of Independence or the Sepoy Mutiny.

question: 1. Which one of the following statements is not correct? [UPSC CSE Pre 1999]
options: ‘Neel Darpan’ was a play based on the exploitation of the indigo farmers
The author of the play ‘Ghashiram Kotwal’s is Vijay Tendulkar
The play “Navanna’ by Nabin Chandra Das was based on the famine of Bengal
Urdu theatre used to depend heavily on Parsi theatre
explanation:
Exp) Option c is the correct answer.
Statement a is correct: “Neel Darpan” was a 19th-century Bengali play by Dinabandhu Mitra, addressing the ruthless exploitation of indigo farmers by British indigo planters in colonial India. The play highlighted the oppressive ‘Neel’ (indigo) system, shedding light on the harsh conditions and exploitation faced by these impoverished farmers.
Statement b is correct: “Ghashiram Kotwal,” a 1972 Marathi play by Vijay Tendulkar, serves as a political satire and historical drama. It critiques the manipulation of power and ideologies, using the lives of Nana Phadnavis and Ghashiram Kotwal to illustrate how those in authority create and discard ideologies for their benefit.
Statement c is incorrect: The play “Navanna,” written by Bijon Bhattacharya in 1944 and staged by IPTA, explores the devastating Bengal famine of 1943, where over 2 million peopie perished from hunger and disease. It follows Pradhan Samaddar, a peasant, depicting the harrowing realities and profound suffering during this tragic period, raising awareness and funds for famine relief.
Statement d is correct: Parsi theatre was the first professional theatre in India and it was very popular among the urban middle class. Urdu theatre borrowed many elements from Parsi theatre, such as the use of music, dance, and spectacle. Urdu playwrights also adapted many Parsi plays into Urdu.

explanation:

Lord Wellesley was the Governor-General of India from 1798 to 1805, and he kept the British flag flying high in India at a time when empires in Europe were crumbling before the might of Napoleon. He pursued an aggressive policy of expansion and consolidation of British power in India, which earned him the nickname of “the Indian Napoleon”. He implemented the system of subsidiary alliances, by which he forced the Indian rulers to accept British protection and supremacy in exchange for their autonomy and sovereignty. He also fought several wars against the enemies of the British, such as the Marathas, the Mysoreans, and the French. He also promoted the cultural and educational development of India, by founding the Fort William College and supporting the Asiatic Society of Bengal.

question: 1. The Governor-General who followed a spirited "Forward" policy towards Afghanistan was: [UPSC CSE Pre 1999]
explanation:
Exp) Option d is the correct answer.
The ‘Forward’ policy of Lord Lytton towards Afghanistan was a misguided attempt to counter the perceived Russian threat in Central Asia. The policy was based on the assumption that the British should pursue an aggressive policy towards Afghanistan in order to prevent the Russians from gaining influence or territory there. The policy involved imposing a British resident and troops in Kabul, demanding concessions from the Afghan ruler, and provoking a war when the Afghans resisted, The policy resulted in the Second Anglo-Afghan War in 1878, which ended in a stalemate and a costly retreat for the British. The policy also alienated the Afghan people, who saw the British as invaders and oppressors.

Important Tips

Key Highlights of Indian Franchise Committee (Lothian Committee):

  • Primary Aim: To establish a suitable foundation for a system of responsible government by framing a new franchise.
  • Electoral Expansion: Proposed an expanded electorate, with 29,382,000 men and 6,620,000 women eligible to choose provincial legislature members, compared to the current figures of 6,792,281 men and 315,651 women.
  • Federal Assembly Electorate: Recommended a federal assembly electorate consisting of 6,864,899 men and 1,578,151 women, a significant increase from the existing combined total of 1,142,948.
  • Reserved Seats for Women: Suggested that between 2 percent and 5 percent of seats in both provincial legislatures and the assembly should be temporarily reserved for women.
  • Educational and Property Qualifications: Proposed the introduction of educational and property qualifications for voters, with special provisions to ensure the enfranchisement of women, untouchables, and labor or other minority groups.
  • Exclusivity to British India: The report dealt exclusively with British India, and the princes of the various states were left to decide on the method of election of their representatives to the federal assembly.

  2. Champaran Satyagrah
  3. Ahmedabad Mill strike

explanation:
Exp) Option b is the correct answer. The correct chronological sequence of the following events in the political life of Mahatma Gandhi is:

  • Champaran Satyagraha: This was the first Satyagraha movement led by Gandhi in India in 1917. It was a farmer's uprising in Bihar against the oppressive Tinkathiya system imposed by the British planters, who forced them to grow indigo and sell it at a low price.
  • Ahmedabad Mill Strike: This was a labour strike led by Gandhi in 1918 in Ahmedabad, Gujarat. It was a protest against the mill owners who refused to increase the wages of the workers after the plague epidemic. Gandhi used the method of hunger strike to support the workers' demand for a 35% increase.
  • Kheda Satyagraha: This was a peasant movement led by Gandhi in 1918 in Kheda district, Gujarat. It was a resistance against the British government's decision to collect full land revenue despite the failure of crops due to drought and famine. Gandhi mobilized the peasants to withhold their payments and demand a suspension of revenue collection.
  • Non-cooperation Movement: This was a mass movement launched by Gandhi in 1920, which lasted till 1922. It was a response to the Rowlatt Act, the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, and the Khilafat issue. It involved boycotting foreign goods, institutions, titles, and honours, promoting swadeshi, education, and self-governance.

question: 1. The first Factory Act for restricting the working hours of women and children, and authorizing local government to make necessary rules was adopted during whose time?
explanation:
Exp) Option c is the correct answer.
Lord Ripon was the Viceroy of India from 1880 to 1884, and he passed the first Factory Act in India in 1881. This Act was based on the terms of the Factory Act of Great Britain, which was enacted in 1837. The first Factory Act in India was a landmark legislation that aimed to regulate the working conditions of women and children in factories. The Act restricted the working hours of women and children to nine hours per day and 48 hours per week. It also authorized the local governments to make rules for the health, safety, and welfare of the workers, such as providing ventilation, lighting, drinking water, latrines, and first-aid facilities.

question:
1. In the contexts of Indian history, which of the following statement is/are correct regarding Vaikom Satyagraha?
  2. It was a satyagraha againsts untouchability and caste discrimination.
  3. Mahatma Gandhi participated in this Satyagraha.
    Select the correct answer using the codes given below. [U.P.P.C.S. (Pre.) 2021]
explanation:
Exp) Option c is the correct answer.
Statement 1 is correct: The Vaikom Satyagraha was a nonviolent agitation for access to the prohibited public environs of the Vaikom Temple in the Kingdom of Travancore, which was known for its rigid and oppressive caste system. It was a movement against untouchability and caste discrimination, as the lower castes (avarnas) were not allowed to enter or even walk on the roads near the temple.
Statement 2 is correct: Mahatma Gandhi participated in this Satyagraha and visited Vaikom in March, 1925. He also supported the cause of temple entry for all Hindus and negotiated with the Regent Maharani Sethu Lakshmi Bai of Travancore. This eventually opened the north, south and west public roads leading to the temple to all castes.

Important Tips

The Vaikom Satyagraha was conceived by T. K. Madhavan, an Ezhava leader and a follower of Sri Narayana Guru, who first raised the question of temple entry of lower castes in an editorial in Deshabhimani newspaper in December 1917.
The movement gained prominence and support from different communities and activists across India, such as the Akalis of Punjab, Christian and Muslim leaders, Chatampi Swamikal and Sree Narayana Guru.
The movement ended on 23rd November 1925 with a compromise between Gandhi and the Regent Maharani, who released all those arrested and opened three public roads to all castes, but kept the eastern road and the temple closed to the lower castes.
Only in 1936, after the Temple Entry Proclamation by Maharaja Chithira Thirunal Balarama Varma, was access to the eastern road and entry into the temple allowed to the lower castes.

question: 1. Who had merged Sikkim in India? [U.P.P.C.S. (Pre) 2020]
explanation:
Exp) Option c is the correct answer.
Lord Dalhousie was the Governor-General of India from 1848 to 1856, and he was responsible for the annexation of Sikkim into the British Empire in 1850. He also annexed many other Indian states using the Doctrine of Lapse, which stated that if a ruler of a dependent state died without a natural heir, the state would be annexed by the British. This policy was widely resented by the Indian princes and contributed to the outbreak of the Indian Rebellion of 1857.

Important Tips

Sikkim did not merge with India until 1975, after a referendum in which the majority of the people voted for joining the Indian Union and abolishing the monarchy.
The last Chogyal (king) of Sikkim was Palden Thondup Namgyal, who had ascended to the throne in 1963.
He faced opposition from pro-democracy groups led by Kazi Lhendup Dorjee, who became the first Chief Minister of Sikkim in 1974.
The merger of Sikkim with India was a result of political and social changes in the region, as well as the strategic interests of India.

explanation:
Exp) Option c is the correct answer.
The Kallar people, primarily associated with the Madurai region, were known for their involvement in various revolts against British India. They were historically known as warriors and peasants and controlled chieftaincies in the region. British sources often referred to them as “soldiers out of work.” Kallar chieftaincies controlled areas north and west of Madurai, and they were considered sovereign and independent. Despite attempts by the British East India Company to pacify them, Kallar raiding parties continued to pose a significant threat, leading to revolts against British control in 1801. The Kallars were also known for working as watchmen in villages, but their practices and abuses led to tensions and movements against their authority, resulting in their classification as a “Criminal Tribe” in 1918.

The correct chronological order of the events is:
3. First Anglo-Sikh War (1845-46): The First Anglo-Sikh War of 1845-46 saw the Sikh Empire's partial subjugation, cession of Jammu & Kashmir to British suzerainty. The war resulted from the Sikh Empire's internal turmoil and British military buildup near Punjab, culminating in battles like Ferozeshah and Sobraon. Treaty terms led to British control over the Sikh Empire's government.
2. Santhal Revolt (1855): The Santhal Rebellion, also known as Santhal Hool, was a revolt by the Santhal tribal people against the British East India Company's oppressive zamindari system in Bengal Presidency. The rebellion took place on 30 June 1855 and was led by four Murmu Brothers — Sidhu, Kanhu, Chand, and Bhairav.
3. Lord Lytton’s Delhi Darbar (1877): In 1876, Queen Victoria in addition to her title of ‘Queen of Great Britain and Ireland’ assumed the title of ‘Empress of India’. The Viceroy, Lord Lytton was asked to proclaim this on her behalf throughout India. He decided to hold an Imperial Assemblage at Delhi on 1st January 1877 for this purpose.
4. Ilbert Bill Controversy (1883): The Ilbert Bill of 1883 aimed to allow Indian judges to preside over trials of British and European subjects in session courts. The controversy arose from racial prejudices, with Europeans vehemently opposing the idea of being tried by Indian judges. A compromise was reached requiring at least half the jury to be European, deepening British-Indian tensions and paving the way for the Indian National Congress and the freedom struggle.

Important Tips

Delhi Durbar:
The Delhi Durbar was a grand assembly organized by the British in Delhi, inspired by Mughal terminology, to commemorate the succession of an Emperor or Empress of India.
Occurring thrice during British colonial rule, it took place in 1877, 1903, and 1911 when the British Empire was at its zenith.
Each Durbar marked a significant coronation event: the first proclaimed Queen Victoria as the Empress of India with the title “Kaisar-i-Hind.”
The second confirmed King Edward VII as the Emperor of India, while the third celebrated King George V's ascension.
King George V was the sole monarch to personally attend a Durbar.
Despite Calcutta being the capital of British India, Lord Lytton, the Governor-General in 1877, selected a location just outside old Delhi for the first Durbar, emphasizing the cultural significance of the former Mughal capital to Indians.

question: 1. Which one of the following statements is not correct about Rabindranath Tagore? [U.P.P.C.S. (Mains) 2013]
options: He sang the glories of ancient India and its culture.
He considered Shivaji and Guru Govind Singh as nation builders.
Many of his songs refute the heroism of Marathas.
He favoured some aspects of the Swadeshi Movement.
explanation:
Exp) Option c is the correct answer.
Rabindranath Tagore, a celebrated poet and philosopher, did not create songs or works that refute the heroism of the Marathas. In fact, he composed a poem titled “Shivaji Utsav” in 1904, which celebrated the valiant Maratha warrior-king, Chhatrapati Shivaji. This poem highlighted Shivaji’s efforts to unify India and resist foreign occupation, particularly the Mughals. Tagore used Shivaji’s bravery and determination as a source of inspiration for the freedom struggle against British colonial rule. Tagore’s literary contributions consistently emphasized heroism and the collective effort needed to combat oppression, including British colonial rule in India.

Important Tips

Rabindranath Tagore’s political views:
Rabindranath Tagore’s political views were characterized by a complex and ambivalent stance, reflecting the nuanced political landscape of his time:
Critique of Swadeshi Movement: He shunned the Swadeshi movement, criticizing it in his 1925 essay “The Cult of the Charkha,” aligning this with elements of Gandhism and the Non-Cooperation Movement. In response to the British proposal to partition Bengal in 1904, Tagore proposed an alternative solution in his lecture “Swadeshi Samaj” advocating a self-help-based reorganization of rural Bengal. However, he was supportive of some economic aspects of the Swadeshi movement, such as the promotion of indigenous industries, but he advocated for a holistic, long-term development approach rather than endorsing short-term methods like boycotting foreign goods and burning foreign clothes.
Denunciation of Nationalism: Tagore strongly denounced nationalism as one of humanity’s greatest problems. He viewed it as a mechanical and selfish endeavor, emphasizing the need for purposeful education over blind revolution.
Vision of East-West Unity: During his extensive travels, Tagore developed a vision of East-West unity, striving fora harmonious coexistence of cultures and nations.
Support for Indian Independence: Despite his reservations, Tagore wrote songs in support of the Indian independence movement and renounced his knighthood in protest against the Amritsar massacre in 1919.
Conflict Resolution: He played a pivotal role in resolving disputes within the Indian independence movement, including the issue of separate electorates for untouchables, mediating between Gandhi and Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar.
Educational Reforms: Tagore criticized the rote-oriented educational system introduced by the British Raj in India. His experimental school at Santiniketan focused on holistic education and became a magnet for scholars, artists, and musicians.
Page 47

Important Tips

The Ahmedabad Strike was triggered by the mill owners’ decision to withdraw the plague bonus that was given to the workers during the epidemic of 1917. The workers demanded a 50% increase in wages to cope with the wartime inflation, but the mill owners were only willing to offer a 20% increase.
Gandhi advised the workers to go on @ peaceful strike and demand a 35% increase in wages, which he considered reasonable and fair.
The strike lasted for 21 days, during which Gandhi tried to negotiate with the mill owners, but they refused to budge. He then decided to go on a fast unto death to strengthen the workers’ resolve and to put moral pressure on the mill owners.
Gandhi's fast had a profound impact on both the workers and the mill owners. The workers remained united and disciplined, while the mill owners felt guilty and ashamed. On the fourth day of his fast, the mill owners agreed to refer the matter to a tribunal, which awarded a 35% increase in wages to the workers.

Important Tips

Curzon-Kitchener controversy:

  • It was a major conflict between the Viceroy of India, Lord Curzon, and the Commander-in-Chief of the British Indian Army, Lord Kitchener, in the early 20th century.
  • The Curzon-Kitchener controversy arose from a disagreement over the status and role of the military member of the Viceroy’s executive council, who was responsible for advising the Viceroy on military matters and controlling the army supply and logistics.
  • Lord Kitchener wanted to abolish this office and bring all the military affairs under his own authority, while Lord Curzon opposed this idea and defended the existing system of dual control.
  • The controversy ended with the resignation of Lord Curzon in August 1905, after he failed to secure the support of the home government for his position. Lord Kitchener emerged as the victor of the conflict, and he succeeded in abolishing the office of the military member and reorganizing the army department according to his wishes.

  • Subordinate union policy (1858-1935 AD): This policy sought to appease and co-opt the Indian states by granting them some privileges and recognising their rights and titles. Some examples of this policy were the Queen's Proclamation of 1858, the Chamber of Princes in 1921, and the Indian States Agency in 1936
  • The policy of equal union (1935-1947 AD): This policy envisaged a federal structure for India, where the Indian states would have equal status and representation with the provinces in 4 central legislature and executive. Nehru favored heavy industrialization as a means to modernize India andbelieved in the importance of building a strong industrial base for economic development. In contrast, Gandhi was critical of heavy industrialization, emphasizing. self-reliance, cottage industries, and rural development. Gandhi’s focus was on rural empowerment and sustainability, while Nehru advocated for rapid industrial growth and urbanization to propel India forward as an industrialized nation.

Important Tips

Differences in Viewpoints between Gandhi and Nehru:
Approach to Non-violence:
Gandhi: Embraced non-violence (Ahimsa) as a core principle, considering it the ultimate weapon for achieving social and political change.
Nehru: While appreciating non-violence’s moral aspects, he didn’t view it as a practical method in all situations and believed in the need for coercive authority to maintain law and order.
Economic Vision:
Gandhi: Advocated for small-scale and cottage industries like Khadi to address poverty and unemployment, emphasizing self-sufficiency and rural development.
Nehru: Supported heavy industrialization and large scale industries, aiming for rapid modernization and technological advancement, even if it meant embracing Western science and technology.
Role of Religion:
Gandhi: Integrated religion and morality into politics, emphasizing truth (Satya) and non-violence (Ahimsa) as the foundation of life. He sought moral regeneration.
Nehru: Promoted secularism and scientific thinking, separating religion from politics. He believed the Congress should focus on political and economic spheres.
Freedom and Equality:
Gandhi: Focused on liberty and envisioned a stateless society with unrestricted individual freedom and minimal state interference.
Nehru: Emphasized equality, advocating for the rationing of freedom to ensure equitable distribution among all members of society. He believed in a strong state to achieve socialist goals.
Western Influence:
Gandhi: Opposed Western civilization, seeking to banish it from India while retaining Britishers as friends in service of the country.
Nehru: Wanted to drive out British colonial rule but appreciated Western culture and civilization.
Role of State:
Gandhi: Preferred a passive role for the state in his vision of autonomous village republics.
Nehru: Advocated for state intervention and control, especially in economic planning, to achieve socialist objectives.

Patel mobilized the peasants to withhold their payments and demand a reduction of the revenue. Lord Curzon was the Viceroy of India from 1899 to 1905, and he passed the Ancient Monuments Preservation Act in 1904. He initiated several projects to repair and renovate some of the famous monuments, such as the Taj Mahal, the Qutub Minar, and the Ajanta Caves.

Important Tips

Ancient Monuments Preservation Act 1904:

  • The Act defined an ancient monument as any structure, erection, or monument, or any tumulus or place of interment, or any cave, rock-sculpture, inscription or monolith, which is of historical, archaeological or artistic interest, or any remains thereof.
  • The Act gave the British government the power to declare any ancient monument as a protected monument, and to acquire rights in or guardianship of such monument from its owner or custodian.
  • The Act also provided for the preservation of ancient monuments by agreement with their owners, and for the compulsory purchase of ancient monuments in certain cases.
  • The Act also authorized the government to control the traffic in antiquities and the moving of sculptures, carvings or like objects.
  • The Act also empowered the government to notify areas as protected for archaeological excavation, and to make rules for regulating such excavation

question: 1. Which one of the following sessions of Indian National Congress was for the first time attended by M.K. Gandhi: [U.P.P.C.S. (Spl) (Mains) 2004]
explanation:
Exp) Option b is the correct answer.
Mahatma Gandhi attended the Calcutta session of Indian National Congress in the year 1901 for the first time. He was then a young lawyer who had recently returned from South Africa. He was impressed by the speeches of Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Dadabhai Naoroji, and others at the session. He also met some of the prominent leaders of the Congress, such as Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal, and Lala Lajpat Rai. He later wrote in his autobiography, “The Congress session in Calcutta left a deep impression on my mind and enhanced my estimation of the Congress.” The Calcutta session of 1901 was presided by Dinshaw E. Wacha, a Parsi leader and a close associate of Dadabhai Naoroji.

Important Tips

Lucknow Session, 1916: This was the session where the Indian National Congress and the All-India Muslim League reached an agreement known as the Lucknow Pact, which aimed to secure constitutional reforms and communal harmony. The session also marked the reunion of the moderate and extremist factions of the Congress. The session was presided by Ambica Charan Mazumdar.
Amritsar Session, 1919: This was the session where the Indian National Congress condemned the Jallianwala Bagh massacre and the martial law imposed in Punjab by the British. The session also rejected the Montague-Chelmsford Reforms as inadequate and disappointing, and endorsed the non-cooperation movement initiated by Mahatma Gandhi. The session was presided by Motilal Nehru.
Nagpur Session, 1920: This was the session where the Indian National Congress adopted some important organizational changes, such as setting up a Congress Working Committee, forming provincial committees on linguistic basis, and reducing the entry fee. The session also confirmed the non-cooperation movement as its main programme and changed its goal from self-government to swaraj. The session was presided by C. Vijayaraghavachariar

He claimed that the Maharaja had failed to protect his subjects from the oppression and extortion of his officials, and that he had neglected the public works and education in his state. He also accused him of being hostile to the British and of conspiring with their enemies, such as the Marathas and the Pindaris. He therefore deposed the Maharaja and placed him under British supervision in a palace in Mysore city. He also appointed a British commissioner to manage the affairs of the state, and introduced several reforms in the administration, revenue, judiciary, and education sectors.

question: 1. Who wrote the famous song ‘Saare Jahan Se Achcha Hindustan Hamara’? [U.P.P.C.S. (Mains) 2004]
explanation:
Exp) Option c is the correct answer.
The renowned poet Sir Muhammad Iqbal wrote the famous song “Saare Jahan Se Achcha Hindustan Hamara” in 1905. This song, often referred to as “Tarana-e-Hindi”, is a patriotic ghazal in Urdu. It played a significant role as a symbol of resistance against British rule during the Indian independence movement. This anthem celebrates India and advocates for unity among people from diverse communities. It remains a popular patriotic song in India and is informally regarded as the nation’s anthem.

Important Tips

Muhammad Iqbal, often referred to as the “Poet of the East,” made significant contributions to literature in multiple languages, primarily Persian, Urdu, and English.
literary works of Muhammad Iqbal:
Persian Works:
“Asrar-i-Khudi” (Secrets of the Self) in 1915, focused on the concept of “Khudi” or “Self” from a religious Perspective.
“Rumuz-i-Bekhudi” (Hints of Selflessness) in 1917 emphasized the Islamic way of life and self-sacrifice for the nation.
“Payam-e-Mashriq” (The Message of the East) in 1924, inspired by Goethe, highlighted the importance of spirituality and morality in the face of materialism.
Urdu Works:
“Bang-e-Dara” (The Call of the Marching Bell) in 1924 contained patriotic and nature-themed poems.
“Bal-e-Jibril” (Wings of Gabriel) in 1935, inspired by Spain, conveyed strong religious passion.
“Zarb-i-Kalim” (The Rod of Moses) in 1936, serving as his political manifesto, critiqued materialism and injustice.
English Works:
“The Development of Metaphysics in Persia” in 1908 explored Persian ideology and Islamic Sufism.
“The Reconstruction of Religious Thought in Islam” in 1930 addressed philosophy, spirituality, and political and social problems.
Punjabi Works:
Wrote poems like “Piyaara Jedi” and “Baba Bakri Wala” in Punjabi.

subject: Modern History
question: 1. Who said, “Political Freedom is the life-breath of a nation”? [U.P.P.C.S. (Mains) 2004]
explanation:
Exp) Option b is the correct answer.
The quote, “Political freedom is the life-breath of a nation. To attempt social reform, educational reform, industrial expansion, the moral improvement of the race without aiming first and foremost at political freedom, is the very height of ignorance and futility,” is attributed to Aurobindo Ghosh. This quote underscores the fundamental importance of political freedom as the foundation upon which other reforms and improvements in society, education, industry, and morality can be built. Ghosh’s belief in the primacy of political freedom was a central tenet of his philosophy and his commitment to India’s struggle for independence.

Important Tips

Aurobindo Ghose:

  • Aurobindo Ghose, born in Calcutta on August 15, 1872, was a multifaceted figure: yogi, seer, philosopher, poet, and Indian nationalist.
  • From 1902 to 1910 he partook in the struggle to free India from the British. As a result of his political activities, he was imprisoned in 1908 (Alipore Bomb case).
  • Two years later he left British India and found refuge in the French colony of Pondichéry (Puducherry), where he devoted himself for the rest of his life to the development of his “integral” yoga with an aim of a fulfilled and spiritually transformed life on earth.
  • He established the Sri Aurobindo Ashram in Pondichéry in 1926.
  • He believed that the basic principles of matter, life, and mind would be succeeded through terrestrial evolution by the principle of supermind as an intermediate power between the two spheres of the infinite and the finite.
  • He authored various literary works, including “Bande Mataram,” “Bhagavad Gita and Its Message,” “The Future Evolution of Man,” “Rebirth and Karma,” and “Savitri: A Legend and a Symbol.”

Lord Mayo was the Viceroy of India from 1869 to 1872, and he was murdered by a convict named Sher Ali Afridi on 8 February 1872, when he was visiting the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

Important Tips

  • He chose Lord Mayo as his target, and attacked him when he was returning to his boat after inspecting the prison facilities. Lord Mayo died shortly after from his wounds.
  • Sher Ali Afridi was immediately arrested and confessed to his crime. He was hanged on 11 March 1872

Exp) Option b is the correct answer.
The twin principles of Mahatma Gandhi’s Ram Rajya were truth and non-violence. This is consistent with Gandhi's philosophy of satyagraha, which means holding on to truth or the force of truth. Gandhi believed that truth and non-violence are the highest values and the foundation of an ideal society. He said, “Truth is God and non-violence is the means of realizing Him”. He also said, “Non-violence is the law of our species as violence is the law of the brute”, Gandhi practiced and preached truth and non-violence throughout his life, and inspired millions of people to follow his path.

Important Tips

Ram Rajya of Gandhi is the name given to the ideal form of governance that Mahatma Gandhi envisioned for India.
Gandhi’s Ram Rajya implied a radical transformation of the social, economic, and political structures of India.
He advocated for a decentralized and democratic system of self-governance, where the people would have equal rights and opportunities, and where the state would be minimal and non-coercive.
He also envisioned a society where there would be no exploitation, oppression, or violence, and where everyone would live in harmony with nature and each other.

subject: Modern History
question: 1. Who established the judicial organization in India? [U.P.P.C.S. (Pre) 1991]
explanation:
Exp) Option b is the correct answer.
Lord Cornwallis is credited with establishing the judicial organization in India. He introduced significant reforms in the Indian judicial system during his tenure as Governor General of India from 1786 to 1793. These reforms were aimed at making the judicial system more efficient, impartial, and accessible to the people.

Important Tips

Lord Cornwallis introduced the following changes in the judicial system:

  • He separated the executive and the judiciary functions of the district collectors, who were previously responsible for both revenue collection and civil justice.
  • He created a new hierarchy of civil courts, with the district judge at the bottom, four provincial courts of appeal in the middle, and the Sadar Diwani Adalat (the Supreme Court of Bengal) at the top.
  • He appointed Indian judges, known as munsifs and amins, to preside over the district courts, while European judges were appointed to the higher courts.
  • He introduced a uniform code of laws for civil cases, based on Hindu and Muslim laws, and compiled by a committee of pandits and qazis.
  • He also reformed the criminal justice system by establishing six circuit courts, each headed by a British judge and assisted by an Indian law officer, to try serious criminal cases.
  • He abolished the judicial powers of the zamindars (landlords) and transferred them to the Company’s courts

question: 1. What was the common relationship between Katherine Mayo, Aldous Huxley, Charles Andrews and William Digby? [56th to 59th B.P.S.C. (Pre) 2015]
options: They wrote commentaries on the condition of India during the British rule
They were supporters of the Indian National Movement
They were opponents of the Indian National Movement
explanation:
Exp) Option a is the correct answer.
Katherine Mayo, Aldous Huxley, Charles Andrews, and William Digby all wrote commentaries or works related to the condition of India during the British colonial period. Mayo’s “Mother India” was a critical examination of Indian society, Huxley’s writings included reflections on Indian philosophy and society, Andrews was an advocate for Indian independence and wrote about Indian issues, and Digby wrote about the Great Famine in India and later worked on Indian political reform.

Important Tips

Katherine Mayo (1867-1940) was an American historian and nativist known for her advocacy of American nativism, opposition to non-white and Catholic immigration, and promotion of racist stereotypes. She also authored “Mother India” (1927), a highly critical book on Indian society, criticized as Indophobic by Mahatma Gandhi and others.
Aldous Huxley (1894-1963) was an English writer and philosopher, known for his extensive bibliography encompassing novels, non-fiction, essays, and poems. He explored philosophical mysticism, universalism, and authored works like “The Perennial Philosophy?” highlighting Western and Eastern mysticism commonalities. He also penned “Brave New World” (dystopia) and “Island” (utopia), envisioning alternate societies.
Charles Freer Andrews (1871-1940) was an Anglican priest, missionary, and advocate for Indian independence. He forged close bonds with Rabindranath Tagore and Mahatma Gandhi, convincing Gandhi to return to India from South Africa. Gandhi affectionately called him “Christ's Faithful Apostle” (C.EA) and his students named him “Deenabandhu” (Friend of the Poor). Charles Freer Andrews, engaged in the Christian Social Union, sought to harmonize Gospel principles with justice. He joined the Cambridge Mission to Delhi in 1904, opposing British racism and supporting Indian political causes. Andrews aided in resolving the 1913 cotton workers’ strike in Madras.
William Digby, a British author and humanitarian, worked in India during the Great Famine of 1876-78, advocating for relief and criticizing British policies. He engaged in liberal politics, pushing for Indian reform.

    Statement II: Indian nationalism as a response to western imperialism was ‘like all such responses, shaped by what it was responding to.
    Code: [CAPF 2017]
options: Both the statements are individually true and statement II is the correct explanation of statement I.
Both the statements are individually true, but statement II is not the correct explanation of statement I.

Statement I is false, but Statements II is true.
explanation:
Exp) Option a is the correct answer.
Statement I is correct: The statement is based on the argument of Partha Chatterjee, a prominent postcolonial scholar. He claimed that nationalism in India was a ‘derivative discourse’ from the West, but also ‘different’ in its content and form. He argued that Indian nationalists adopted the political and ideological framework of western nationalism, but also modified it to suit their own cultural and historical context. The Indian nationalists drew inspiration from the ancient and medieval history of India, as well as from the contemporary movements of nationalism and democracy in Europe and America. They also adapted and modified these ideas to suit the Indian context and culture
Statement II is correct: Statement II explains that Indian nationalism was shaped by its response to Western imperialism, which is a common phenomenon when nations respond to external pressures. Many Indian leaders, including Gandhi and Nehru, were educated in the West and were exposed to Western political and philosophical ideas, such as democracy, freedom, and self-determination.
Taken together, statement II provides an explanation for statement I by highlighting the connection between Indian nationalism and its response to Western imperialism.

question: 1. Which revolutionary made this statement: “Avenge the blood of Indian Martyrs. Use your sword fo liberate your motherland. Stand up against the entire Anglo-American enemy” [Chhattisgarh P.C.S. (Pre) 2019]
explanation:
Exp) Option a is the correct answer.
Rash Behari Bose, the revolutionary, made the statement: “avenge the blood of Indian Martyrs. Use your sword to liberate your motherland. Stand up against the entire Anglo-American enemy.” This statement reflected his strong commitment to the cause of Indian independence and his call for armed resistance against British colonial rule. He played a significant role in organizing the Azad Hind Fauj (Indian National Army) and mobilizing Indian soldiers and citizens in the fight for freedom.

Important Tips

Rash Behari Bose:

  • Born on May 25, 1886, in Subaldaha, Bengal, Rash Behari Bose was orphaned at a young age, raised by his maternal aunt.
  • Rash Behari’s patriotism blossomed after reading revolutionary literature, including Bankim Chandra Chatterjee’s “Ananda Math” and Navin Sen’s “Plasir Yudha.” Influenced by teacher Charu Chand in Chandernagore, he embraced revolutionary ideals.
  • The 1905 partition of Bengal triggered Rash Behari’s entry into revolutionary activities, led by Jatin Banerjee.
  • He played a crucial role in the 1912 bomb attack on Lord Hardinge, Viceroy of India.
  • Rash Behari was instrumental in organizing the Ghadar Revolution, mobilizing thousands of Indians, including those from the Ghadar Party in America, Canada, and the Far East
  • Rash Behari escaped to Japan in 1915, living under the identity of Raja P.N.T. Tagore.
  • He became a Japanese citizen, married, learned Japanese, and engaged in cultural activities while promoting India’s perspective.
  • Rash Behari, along with Captain Mohan Singh and Sardar Pritam Singh, played akey role in establishing the Indian National Army (Azad Hind Fauj) on September 1, 1942, with the support of the Japanese.
  • Rash Behari Bose passed away on January 21, 1945, in Tokyo, and the Japanese government posthumously honored him with the Second Order of Merit of the Rising Sun.

question: 1. Who had proposed “Party Less Democracy’ in India? [M.P.P.C.S. (Pre) 2019]
explanation:
Exp) Option d is the correct answer.
Jayaprakash Narayan advocated for a “Party Less Democracy” in India. He believed that while parties, elections, and the constitution were crucial for democracy, true democracy would only flourish when moral values and spiritual qualities were ingrained in the public. He argued that the party system often led to a disconnect between people and their representatives, emphasizing the need for a more direct and morally grounded democratic process.

Important Tips

Jayaprakash Narayan proposed four key suggestions for implementing a partyless democracy:
Abolish Political Parties: Narayan recommended the elimination of political parties from the democratic system. Instead, he advocated for direct elections of candidates at all levels, from villages to the central government. Each gram sabha would elect two representatives to the electoral council for their constituency, where candidates for state legislatures or the central parliament would be proposed and supported in open meetings, ensuring public participation. Candidates with over 30% of the vote would become representatives.
Free Sarvodaya Society from Party Politics: Narayan emphasized the need to separate the Sarvodaya society from party politics, allowing it to operate independently.
Invite All Parties to Participate in Sarvodaya Work: He suggested inviting all political parties to participate in Sarvodaya activities, fostering cooperation and ending the divisive spirit of political parties.
Candidates to Break from Parties After Election: Narayan proposed that elected candidates should dissociate themselves from their respective parties after winning elections. This would allow them to represent the people independently and avoid the constraints of party ideologies and discipline.

subject: Modern History
question: 1. Which part of India remained under Portuguese control after 15th August 1947? [M.P.P.C.S. (Pre) 2010]
explanation:
Exp) Option a is the correct answer.
After August 15, 1947, the part of India that remained under Portuguese control was Goa. Goa was a Portuguese colony and continued to be under Portuguese rule until it was annexed by India in December 1961. Portugal recognized Indian control over Goa in a treaty signed on December 31, 1974, following the Carnation Revolution and the fall of the Estado Novo regime in Portugal.

Important Tips

Timeline of Goa’s Integration into the Indian Union:

  • Post-Independence Relations (1947-1949): After India gained independence in 1947, diplomatic relations were established with Portugal in 1949.
  • Deterioration of Relations (1950): Relations between India and Portugal deteriorated due to Portugal’s refusal to surrender its enclaves on India’s west coast, including Goa, Daman and Diu, and Dadra and Nagar Haveli.
  • Recognition as Overseas Province (1951): In 1951, Portugal changed its constitution, recognizing Goa as an overseas province rather than a colonial possession. This move was seen as an attempt to invoke NATO’s collective security clause in case of an Indian attack.
  • Diplomatic Break (1955): By 1955, diplomatic relations between India and Portugal had been severed, leading to a crisis.
  • Liberation of Goa (1961): In 1961, India launched Operation Vijay on December 19th, leading to the annexation of Daman and Diu, as well as Goa, and the end of Portuguese rule over these enclaves.
  • Operation Vijay involved air, sea and land strikes for over 36 hours, and was a decisive victory for India, ending 451 years of rule by Portugal over its remaining enclaves in India. The engagement lasted two days, and twenty-two Indians and thirty Portuguese were killed in the fighting.

The Congress session demanded a responsible government and the protection of civil liberties within the states.

Important Tips

  • The Saddler Commission, chaired by Dr. Michael E. Saddler, was appointed by the Government of India in 1917. It aimed to study and proposed reforms for Calcutta University and the broader education system. The commission recommended a 12-year school course, separating secondary and intermediate education, and emphasized the need for universities to focus on higher education.
  • English higher education in India can be said to have begun with the establishment of Hindu College in Calcutta in 1817, the first ‘Europanized’ institution of higher learning in Asia. The first three universities of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras, established in 1857 were modeled on London.

subject: Geography
question:
1. Consider the following countries:
    I. United Kingdom
    II. Denmark
    III. New Zealand
    IV. Australia
    V. Brazil

How many of the above-countries have more than four time zones?
explanation:
Exp) Option b is the correct answer.
Different countries may span multiple time zones due to their wide east-west geographical extent or because of overseas territories. However, not all large countries have more than four actual operating time zones.

Option I is correct. UK has 9 time zones
The UK spans nine time zones—from the Pitcairn Islands (UTC-08:00) to the British Indian Ocean Territory (UTC+06:00)—including places like the Cayman Islands, Bermuda, and Gibraltar. The main UK region, around London, is in the UTC+00:00 time zone, showing the lasting impact of GMT/UTC in global navigation.

Option II is correct. Denmark has 5 time zones.
Denmark spans five time zones, including Greenland, which operates at UTC-04:00, while the main territory operates at UTC+01:00. Greenland itself has three additional time zones, mostly at UTC-03:00. Near the Arctic Circle, time becomes fluid, with summers of perpetual daylight and winters of prolonged darkness, making time zones crucial for communication and balance.

Option III is correct. New Zealand has 5 time zones.
The UTC line between New Zealand’s islands of Niue and Tokelau seems arbitrary given their proximity. Despite a 24-hour difference justified by 700 miles of longitude separation, inhabitants practically experience the ‘same day.’ This Pacific location was chosen in 1884 to avoid global frustration, although the line could have been drawn elsewhere, such as between Colorado and Kansas or Austria and Hungary. New Zealand's three other time zones cover its main territory, the Cook Islands, and the Chatham Islands.

Option IV is correct.- Australia has 9 time zones.
Australia’s expansive territory includes its mainland and nearby islands. Settlement on the mainland dates back thousands of years, with British control established in 1788 through convict colonisation. Australia claims islands like Heard and McDonald Islands (UTC+05:00), Christmas Island (UTC+07:00), and Norfolk Island (UTC+11:00), while its mainland operates within time zones ranging from UTC+08:00 to UTC+10:00.

Option V is incorrect. Brazil has 4 time zones.
Brazil spans four time zones due to its immense size and inclusion of adjacent islands. The easternmost zone, UTC-02:00, covers the Rocas Atoll and Saint Peter and Saint Paul Archipelago. Moving west, the Amazonas territory falls under UTC-05:00, known for its vast jungle. This extends to the segment governed by UTC-04:00, while the southeastern region follows UTC-03:00.

subject: Geography
question:
1. Consider the following statements:
    I. Anadyr in Siberia and Nome in Alaska are a few kilometers from each other, but when people are waking up and getting set for breakfast in these cities, it would be different days.
    II. When it is Monday in Anadyr, it is Tuesday in Nome.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation:
Exp) option a is the correct answer.
Anadyr is a town located in the far eastern part of Russia in the region of Chukotka, and Nome is a town in western Alaska, USA. Although they are geographically close — separated only by the Bering Strait — they lie on opposite sides of the International Date Line (IDL). The IDL is an imaginary line, roughly along the 180° longitude, where the calendar date changes by one day when crossed.

Statement I is correct. Anadyr in Russia and Nome in Alaska are geographically close and separated only by the Bering Strait. However, they lie on opposite sides of the International Date Line (IDL). This means that although it may be the same clock time, say, 8:00 AM in both places, the calendar date would be different. For example, if it’s Monday morning in Anadyr, it would still be Sunday morning in Nome. The IDL causes this one-day difference despite the small distance between the two locations.

Statement II is incorrect. When it is Monday in Anadyr, it cannot be Tuesday in Nome. In fact, it’s the reverse. Nome lags behind Anadyr by a day. So if it is Monday in Anadyr, it is still Sunday in Nome. The International Date Line adds a day as one travels westward, and subtracts a day as one travels eastward — which makes Russia (west of the IDL) ahead of the U.S. (east of the IDL).

  2. Asteroids are small rocky planetoids, while comets are formed of frozen gases held together by rocky and metallic material.
  3. Asteroids are found mostly between the orbits of Jupiter and Mars, while comets are found mostly between Venus and Mercury.
  4. Comets show a perceptible glowing tail, while asteroids do not.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation:
Exp) Option b is the correct answer.
Asteroids, sometimes called minor planets, are rocky, airless remnants left over from the early formation of our solar system about 4.6 billion years ago. Comets are cosmic snowballs of frozen gases, rock, and dust that orbit the Sun.

Statement 1 and 3 are correct. Asteroids are small, rocky objects that orbit the Sun. Comets are frozen leftovers from the formation of the solar system composed of dust, rock and ices. They range from a few miles to tens of miles wide, but as they orbit closer to the sun, they heat up and spew gases and dust into a glowing head that can be larger than a planet. This material forms a tail that stretches millions of miles.

Statement 2 is incorrect. The asteroid belt is located roughly between the orbits of the planets Jupiter and Mars. Comets are not limited to any specific region; they are spread all over the solar system.

question: 1. Who of the following scientists proved that the stars with mass less than 1.44 times the mass of the Sun end up as White Dwarfs when they die?
explanation:
Exp) Option b is the correct answer.
Subrahmanyam Chandrasekhar, an Indian-born scientist is most famous for coming up with the theory that explains the death of the universe’s most massive stars. Chandrasekhar showed that it is impossible for a white dwarf star, which is supported solely by a degenerate gas of electrons, to be stable if its mass is greater than 1.44 times the mass of the Sun. If such a star does not completely exhaust its thermonuclear fuel, then this limiting mass may be slightly larger.
All direct mass determinations of actual white dwarf stars have resulted in masses less than the Chandrasekhar limit. A star that ends its nuclear-burning lifetime with a mass greater than the Chandrasekhar limit must become either a neutron star or a black hole.
Before Chandrasekhar, scientists assumed that all stars collapsed into white dwarfs when they died. He determined this isn’t so.

  3. The albedo of Mercury is much greater than the albedo of the Earth.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation:
Exp) Option a is the correct answer.
Statement 1 is correct: Albedo is the fraction of the incident sunlight that is reflected from the surface of an object. When an object reflects most of the light that hits it, it looks bright and has a high albedo. For example, snow and ice have high albedos. When an object absorbs most of the light that hits it, it looks dark and has a low albedo. For example, asphalt and charcoal have low albedos. The albedo of an object also depends on the wavelength of the light, as some objects may reflect more or less light at different parts of the electromagnetic spectrum.

Statement 2 is incorrect: Mercury, the closest planet to the Sun, has a very low albedo, because it is mainly composed of dark porous rock that reflects very little light. The albedo of Mercury is 0.142, which is lower than the albedo of Earth, which is 0.367. This means that Mercury appears darker than Earth when viewed with reflected light. The albedo of Earth is higher than Mercury’s because Earth has clouds, oceans, ice caps, and vegetation that reflect lighter than Mercury’s barren surface.

question: 1. A ship is moving from the eastern side of Aleutian Islands towards Dutch Harbour. It crosses 180° meridian on 1st January 1999 at 23:30 hr. What time and date will be recorded by the captain of the ship in his diary after one-hour journey from the point of crossing of the meridian?
explanation:
Exp) Option b is the correct answer.
When crossing the International Date Line (IDL), the change in the date and time depends on the direction of travel. If a ship is moving from the eastern side of the Aleutian Islands towards Dutch Harbour (westward), it will gain a day when it crosses the 180° meridian. So, if the ship crosses the meridian on 1st January 1999 at 23:30 hr, after one-hour journey, it will be recorded as January 2, 00:30 hr in the captain’s diary. The ship moves into the next day as it travels westward.

Important Tips

Time and date across IDL:

  • Crossing the IDL results in either gaining or losing a day depending on the direction of travel.
  • Traveling westward across the IDL leads to gaining a day, while traveling eastward results in losing a day.
  • Example: If someone travels eastward from Wake Island to the Hawaiian Islands on June 25, they will shift their calendar back to June 24 upon crossing the IDL. Traveling westward in the opposite direction would mean arriving at Wake Island on June 26.
  • When moving westward from the IDL, travelers gain one hour for every 15° of longitude crossed.
  • Travelers moving eastward lose one hour for every 15° of longitude crossed.
  • If travelers journey westward without adjusting their time by one hour for every 15° meridian, they will find that they have gained an extra day when returning to their starting point.

Countries according to their standard time from ahead of GMT to behind GMT are as follows:

  • Japan (UTC+09:00) - Standard Time in Japan is 9 hours ahead of GMT.
  • Iraq (UTC+03:00) - Standard Time in Iraq is 3 hours ahead of GMT.
  • Greece (UTC+02:00) - Standard Time in Greece is 2 hours ahead of GMT.
  • Cuba (UTC-05:00) - Standard Time in Cuba is 5 hours behind of GMT.
  • Costa Rica (UTC-06:00) - Standard Time in Costa Rica is 6 hours behind of GMT.

Important Tips

Greenwich Mean Time (GMT):

  • GMT is the mean solar time at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, London, counted from midnight.
  • GMT has been calculated in different ways in the past, including being calculated from noon. This historical variation means that it cannot specify a particular time without context.
  • GMT is also used as one of the names for the time zone UTC+00:00. In the United Kingdom, it is the basis for civil time.
  • English speakers often use GMT interchangeably with Coordinated Universal Time (UTC).
  • For navigation purposes, GMT is considered equivalent to UT1, which is the modern form of mean solar time at 0° longitude. However, there can be slight differences (up to 0.9 seconds) between GMT and UTC. Thus, GMT should not be used for applications requiring high precision due to variations caused by Earth's elliptical orbit and axial tilt.
  • Noon GMT is rarely the exact moment when the Sun crosses the Greenwich Meridian and reaches its highest point in the sky due to Earth’s uneven angular velocity. This event can occur up to 16 minutes before or after noon GMT, and the annual average of these moments is what GMT represents, explaining the “mean” in “Greenwich Mean Time.”

question: 1. A plane starts flying from 30° northern latitude and 50° eastern longitude and lands at the opposite end of the earth, where will it land-
explanation:
Exp) Option d is the correct answer.
The opposite end of the Earth from 30° North Latitude, 50° East Longitude is 30° South Latitude, 130° West Longitude. When a plane aims to reach the opposite end of its starting point, it is essentially trying to reach the antipodal point of its initial location. The antipode of any location on Earth is the point that is diametrically opposite to it on Earth's surface, and a straight line connecting the two points would pass through the center of the Earth.
To find the antipode of a given location on Earth, you need to consider the geographic coordinates (latitude and longitude). If the starting point is at 30 degrees northern latitude and 50 degrees eastern longitude, then the antipodal point would have:

  • The latitude would change to its opposite, so 30 degrees northern latitude becomes 30 degrees southern latitude.
  • The longitude would change to its opposite by adding or subtracting 180 degrees, so 50 degrees eastern longitude becomes 50 degrees - 180 degrees = -130 degrees western longitude.
